entries.title: Lincoln Park residents plan rally after ComEd rejects alternate substation sites
entries.summary: <p>More neighbors are joining the Diversey Community Coalition’s call to block a 1-acre ComeEd substation in Lincoln Park, after the utility rejected more than a dozen alternative sites for the project.</p><p>The Diversey Community Coalition, a neighborhood group created in response to ComEd’s proposal, worked alongside local elected officials, neighbors and consultants to propose 14 other locations for ComEd’s planned substation at 1111 W. Diversey Parkway. The utility purchased the land for $11.5 million in 2021, Cook County property records show.</p><p>The coalition argues that ComEd can use a different site that isn’t so closely located near transit, schools and a daycare. </p><p>Its list of properties included a Jewel Osco parking lot on North Clybourn Avenue and a 1.2-acre lot on Diversey Parkway. The coalition shared a map of the properties and updates on the substation during a Wednesday community meeting in Lincoln Park.</p><p>“There's nothing magical about Diversey,” Marie Poppy, co-founder of the Diversey Community Coalition, said during the meeting. “They think it is, but we're saying no."</p><p>ComEd in an August letter doubled down on the Diversey project, saying none of the 14 parcels were viable, citing various reasons from lots being too small, not for sale or not cost effective. </p><p>But one of the alternative sites was a 1.2-acre parcel — the 1111 W. Diversey site is 1.08 acres.</p><p>“ComEd is not being earnest with us,” Poppy said. “If you were at any of the other meetings, they said they want transparency. They want to work with the community. Well, we're not seeing it. We're just not seeing it.”</p><p>ComEd didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The community coalition plans to hold a rally Saturday at 11 a.m. at ComEd’s proposed substation site.</p><p>Diversey Community Coalition co-founder Jim Maggio said the rally's goal is to let people know they want housing — not just for the substation to be blocked.</p><p>"We need to be able to protect what they call equitable transit-oriented development,” Maggio said. “Anything within a half a mile of a transit stop, like the Brown Line Diversey stop, needs to be protected.”</p><p>The utility giant has previously said it’s proposing the substation because of<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2026/05/13/comed-electric-customer-bills-rising-ai-data-centers-pjm-energy-costs" target="_blank" ><u> rising power demand</u></a> on the North Side. It has three substations that serve Lake View, North Center, Uptown and northern Lincoln Park, but those substations are nearing capacity.</p><p>The three substations reached 95% of their allowable capacity this year, according to ComEd. The substations are expected to reach 98% capacity by 2031, with two exceeding their limits.</p><p>But the coalition has questioned why the substation needs to be built at the Diversey location, when the land could be sold to a developer that would build homes. The site is about 735 feet from the Diversey CTA station, making it an equitable transit-oriented development site. </p><p>Streets within half a mile of a CTA or Metra station, or quarter of a mile of a qualifying CTA bus line, are eligible for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/08/15/parking-requirements-cta-metra-transit-affordable-housing-crisis" >transit-oriented development</a> designation, which encourages walkable and high-density projects by offering grants and reduced development costs, according to the city.</p><p>The coalition has just over 2,000 individuals signed up for its newsletter, according to Maggio.</p><p>Neighborhood groups Wrightwood Neighbors Association and Central Lake View Neighbors have joined the coalition’s call for ComEd to abandon the site. The coalition also has the backing of alders Timmy Knudsen (43rd), Bennet Lawson (44th) and Scott Waguespack (32nd), as well as Sen. Sara Feigenholtz and Rep. Ann Williams.</p><p>Knudsen proposed an ordinance to the City Council earlier this summer that would require more oversight and community involvement in “major infrastructure proposals” for projects larger than 0.5 acres or within 600 feet of a residential property. </p><p>Knudsen said Wednesday night that his ordinance was sent to the council’s Rules Committee in an attempt to block it. But Lawson has since put forth a new ordinance that would treat any new substation as a major utility if it’s within 100 feet of residential property and more than 0.5 acres. </p><p>Classifying a substation as a major utility would trigger more community oversight, Knudsen said. Currently, ComEd’s substation is considered a minor utility and can be built by right.</p><p>Feigenholtz said during the meeting that she called Gov. JB Pritzker about the issue. She hopes a bill, similar to Lawson’s ordinance, she introduced earlier this year will be discussed during the Illinois General Assembly’s fall veto session.</p><p>“When I read [ComEd’s] responses and how disrespectful and dismissive they were … is when I made the call,” Feigenholtz said.</p>
entries.author: Abby Miller

entries.title: Blackhawks shut out by Blues in Patrick Kane's lone preseason appearance
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> fans in Chicago will have to wait until the team's regular-season home opener (Oct. 6) to get their first look at Patrick Kane back at the United Center.</p><p>In a rare and somewhat strange moment of collaboration between the marketing department and coaching staff, Kane made his one and only preseason appearance Thursday in the Hawks' 1-0 road loss in St. Louis — with "road" being the critical part.</p><p>He didn't play in the first home preseason game Monday, and it doesn't sound like he'll play in the home preseason finale Saturday, either, in order to build anticipation — and potentially boost ticket prices — for the home opener.</p><p>Although the Hawks sent a mix of NHL and AHL players Thursday, fellow first-line forwards Frank Nazar and Roman Kantserov accompanied Kane to continue building chemistry before the games start counting.</p><p>Their line was the only one that generated consistent offensive chances for the Hawks. Encouragingly, the Kane-Kantserov connection seen in practice did translate into a game format. Backup goalie Arvid Soderblom was the Hawks' best player in the game, making 35 saves.</p><p>Third periods have been the Hawks' worst in all three preseason games so far, in which they're 1-1-1. That will be a trend to monitor entering the regular season, although it could be attributed to their lengthy, tiring camp practices right now.</p><p>The Hawks are expected to dress a mostly NHL lineup Saturday in a rematch against the Blues.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Rocket pass from Kane to get Kantserov a look in tight: <a href="https://t.co/9piNsVA3ox">pic.twitter.com/9piNsVA3ox</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2103283542738571455?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Same old ‘PK’</b></h3><p>The Hawks enter this season utilizing the same unique and somewhat complicated penalty-killing system that worked well for them last year, helping them finish second in the NHL in penalty-killing rate (83.6%).</p><p>The system is a hybrid between the standard "diamond" and "push-down" types. In its initial and most passive forms, it resembles a diamond, but killers are encouraged to aggressively spring outward whenever they sense an opportunity to disrupt the opposing power play.</p><p>The personnel looks significantly different, though, with Jason Dickinson and Connor Murphy now in Edmonton and Ilya Mikheyev now in Tampa.</p><p>Summer additions Cole Smith, Jordan Greenway and Ian Cole as well as rookie Anton Frondell are all expected to play penalty-killing roles, but they're learning the system from scratch right now — which isn't easy.</p><p>Returning killers from last year — including Alex Vlasic, Wyatt Kaiser, Ryan Greene and Frank Nazar — are helping Blashill and assistant coach Michael Peca teach it.</p><p>Sizable portions of several days of camp have been dedicated to special-teams practice, with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/21/blackhawks-power-play-patrick-kane-roman-kantserov-bowen-byram" >Hawks’ power play</a> facing their own penalty kill.</p><p>"We've practiced it a lot on purpose," Blashill said. "Because we think it’s something that [during] the early part of the year, both sides of special teams can help get you points when everybody’s five-on-five game is coming [along more slowly]. I think they’re getting where they’re comfortable."</p><p>They got a lot of work in-game Thursday, going 0-for-5 on the power play but 7-for-7 on the penalty kill.</p><h3><b>Injury updates</b></h3><p>Connor Bedard continues to skate on his own with skills coaches. He has graduated this week into taking slap shots. Blashill said Bedard's return to team practices is "obviously not forthcoming in the next little bit."</p><p>Greenway left practice early Wednesday and didn't participate Thursday due to a lower-body injury, which Blashill deemed day-to-day. Greenway missed tons of time the last two seasons with the Sabres due to hernia problems, so the lower-body designation is slightly worrying.</p>

entries.title: Week 6's top games: Mount Carmel at Brother Rice highlights the slate
entries.summary: <p><b>No. 1 Mount Carmel at No. 4 Brother Rice</b></p><p><b>7:30 p.m. Friday: </b>It’s rivalry week in several conferences around the area, and this is a big one for South Side bragging rights. Mount Carmel (4-1, 1-0 Catholic League Blue) leads the all-time series 43-29, but the teams have split the last 14 games. Both are loaded with Power Four prospects. The Caravan’s headliners include receivers Quentin Burrell (Michigan) and Marshaun Thornton, offensive lineman Chase Clark (Purdue), linebacker Roman Igwebuike (Notre Dame), defensive back Tavares Harrington (Michigan) and defensive linemen Darin Graham (Wisconsin) and Caleb Tucker. Brother Rice (3-2, 0-1) counters with defensive linemen Brayden Parks (Notre Dame) and Kam McGee, safety Jonathan Harrris (Iowa) and tight end Jack McNamara. Senior Rocco Galasso and freshman Sam Holcomb have been a productive quarterback combo.</p><p><b>No. 16 Geneva at No. 6 Batavia</b></p><p><b>7 p.m. Friday: </b>One of the state’s oldest rivalries, dating back to 1912, and likely the best documented, thanks to the ongoing efforts of Batavia historian George H. Scheetz. Geneva (4-1, 3-0 DuKane) leads the series 52-50 with five ties, but Batavia (4-1, 3-0) has won 14 of the last 15 meetings. Both teams have elite passing games this year. Batavia’s Michael Vander Luitgaren, a Wyoming commitment, has completed 77% of his passes for 1,509 yards and 19 touchdowns. Darin Ashiru (39 receptions, 594 yards, five touchdowns) is his top target. Geneva’s Ben Peterson (Eastern Michigan) has thrown for 1,607 yards and 19 touchdowns with 70% accuracy, and Bennett Konkey (Illinois) has 40 catches for 886 yards and 12 touchdowns.</p><p><b>No. 22 Providence vs. Fenwick</b></p><p><b>7 p.m. Friday at Triton: </b>Class 5A top-ranked Providence (4-1, 1-0 Catholic League Orange) is looking for its first win under interim coach Adam Nissen, who was in charge for last week’s loss at Nazareth after the firing of Tyler Plantz. Senior Broden Mackert is one of the state’s top running backs. Iowa commit Jake Thies of Fenwick (4-1, 0-1), a defensive back and running back, is among the state’s best two-way players. Junior Myles Hill is an effective dual-threat quarterback for the defending 6A state champs.</p><p><b>Morgan Park vs. Simeon</b></p><p><b>1:30 p.m. Saturday at Rockne: </b>With Gately Stadium being renovated, this South Side rivalry was relocated to the West Side. Morgan Park (4-1, 2-0 Public League Red Star) has the Public League’s top prospect in senior defensive back Darrell Mattison, an Ole Miss commit. Quarterback Ronald Smith Jr. and running back Will Smith Jr. are a pair of impact players on offense for the Mustangs. Simeon (1-4, 1-1) has a bright future with the sophomore pitch-and-catch duo of quarterback Aki King and receiver Jalonny Billingsley, while defensive linemen Corey Randolph (Boston College) and Brian DeMoss and running back James Bell are top senior prospects.</p><p><b>No. 23 Wheaton North at Wheaton-Warrenville South</b></p><p><b>7 p.m. Friday: </b>Wheaton North (5-0, 2-0 DuKane) has been one of the year’s biggest surprises. A big reason is the play of senior tight end/linebacker Adam Schilling, whose 2025 season was cut short by a knee injury. Senior running back Mac Murray also has been an impact player. Three-sport standout AJ Rogers has put up big numbers for Wheaton-Warrenville South (3-2, 1-1), throwing for 1,382 yards and 10 touchdowns.</p>

entries.title: White Sox players always believed their stunning playoff berth was possible
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — As Trevor Richards, the rubber-armed reliever rescued from years of bouncing between the minors and majors, stepped on first base for the final out on Thursday, his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> teammates reacted in subdued fashion.</p><p>The first team in MLB history to reach the postseason on the heels of three-straight seasons of 100 losses or more, lined up for post-victory handshakes like it was any other win.</p><p>It was a feint.</p><p>“We knew we kinda had to play it chill,” said shortstop Colson Montgomery, donning ski goggles and light years away from caring about tying the MLB single-season strikeout record. “We just knew once we got in the clubhouse, we were all going to go nuts and go crazy. This is just a product of a couple years in the making.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">dance with us 🕺 <a href="https://t.co/swmeWpV42C">pic.twitter.com/swmeWpV42C</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2103259584240722152?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 24, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The turmoil of those years inspired a release beyond what paddling a last-place Royals team 9-1 to clinch — for now — the final American League wild card spot might otherwise inspire.</p><p>“We’ve been chasing this moment for a long time,” said Miguel Vargas, a human mood ring for the White Sox franchise over the last three seasons. “It’s special for us, it’s special for the organization.”</p><p>“This is what we do,” said Sean Burke, surveying the jubilant landscape with a cigar in hand, and scheduled for a start on Friday crucial for the AL Central race.</p><p>As Montgomery’s interview ended, the opening chords of Clarence Carter’s “Strokin’” — the bawdy 80’s funk hit that became the de facto anthem for a Sox offense that shocked the league with best-in-AL production — began to play, inspiring a mob of dancing around clubhouse energizer Mike Vasil.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/-D9jOhxk3xQ?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="White Sox players celebrate their playoff berth in the clubhouse"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“This is what the White Sox are,” Munetaka Murakami said via interpreter. “We’ve come together. This is not the end.”</p><p>About a half hour after reaching base five times, catching nine innings of one-run ball and lifting his fifth home run of an otherwise injury-ravaged season, a shirtless Kyle Teel was being hoisted in the air by Vasil. Efforts for Teel to return the favor were genuine, but quickly abandoned. In the past few days, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/23/white-sox-still-want-the-division-title-but-earning-a-playoff-berth-would-be-everything-davis-martin-chris-getz-jin-wong-miguel-vargas-grant-taylor-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>Sox players assured that their larger goals</u></a> wouldn’t dampen their celebration of a playoff berth, and were as good as their word.</p><p>“This was better than anything I could have ever imagined,” said Davis Martin, as the longest-tenured White Sox player took a moment to watch from the sidelines. “When you’re 6-13, it’s real easy to go ‘we’re still rebuilding, we’re still not ready to compete.’ We didn’t do that.”</p><p>In an age where teams claiming that “nobody believed in us” in their beer-drenched celebratory locker rooms has become a cliche, the White Sox can claim it genuinely, and maybe even internally; in the sense of how quickly it happened.</p><p>There were champagne stains on the shirts of White Sox front office members as well, but they once thought–like everyone else in the sport–they were navigating a methodical return to postseason baseball. The Murakami signing that convinced so many Sox players that the sky was the limit for this year, was once seen as a low-risk, buy-low addition for a team with little to lose.</p><p>Corner a Sox player on when they believed the playoffs were possible, and the answer will be “spring training.” Corner a Sox decision-maker, and the answer might be more nuanced.</p><p>“It happened organically throughout the year,” said manager Will Venable.</p><p>“It doesn't really matter what I think,” said general manager Chris Getz. “Because this group believes.”</p><p>Incredibly, they always did. Burke, who debuted at the end of the wretched, 121-loss 2024 season, has said he thanks God that he’s a member of the Chicago White Sox.</p><p>It was a common feeling on Thursday, but it began earlier.</p><p>“Honestly, man, when I first debuted I felt that way, even though we were terrible,” Burke told the Sun-Times. “We play in one of the best cities in America, one of the most iconic sports teams in the country. I felt it from the start.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Ald. Curtis calls for accountability after security vehicle strikes teen at Ford City Mall
entries.summary: <p>A security guard at the now-shuttered Ford City Mall has been accused of hitting an 18-year-old with his vehicle Monday night after allegedly battering a man with a metal rod in an incident captured on video, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The victims — who spoke to the Sun-Times on condition of anonymity — had been riding Lime e-scooters on a sidewalk near the property around 11 p.m. when a white SUV approached them before a man exited and reached for something from the backseat. One of the riders, a 28-year-old man, tried to talk to the security guard, who, without speaking, allegedly struck him with a metal object.</p><p>The 18-year-old and 28-year-old then fled, with the unidentified security guard following in his vehicle, eventually catching up to them and striking the teen with the car near a gym operating on the mall’s campus. Paramedics treated both at the scene for injuries, according to Chicago police, who said the incident remains under investigation. No arrests have been made. </p><p>“I’ve never had a confrontation with security like that. Usually they’ll just ask you to leave, and we obey that,” the teen said.</p><p>Videos of the encounter, which have amassed tens of thousands of views across social media platforms as of Thursday, show the driver of a white SUV accelerating and hitting the teen, knocking him off the scooter as he continues recording. Both victims had been wearing GoPro cameras and were recording at the time of the incident.</p><p>In a statement, Namdar Realty Group, current owners of Ford City Mall, said it was "disturbed by what they (videos) appear to show."</p><p>"The safety of anyone on our property, regardless of the circumstances, matters to us, and the actions depicted do not reflect mall security protocols nor conduct that ownership condones," the statement said. "We are taking the investigation of this incident very seriously, in collaboration with the Chicago Police Department." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> There’s too much crime going on,” Curtis told the Sun-Times Thursday. “[But] we will not only hold the security company responsible, but Namdar as well, for all their injuries.”</p><p>The teen and man who were injured are self-described urban explorers who often take videos around and inside abandoned buildings across the world. They explained they had just been driving around the lot that night and are used to interacting with security, who generally just ask them to leave. </p><p>In other cases, police are called, and they're issued a trespass order.</p><p>They explained being caught off guard by the hostility, as their interactions with other security guards have been relatively cordial because “our goal isn't to damage or do anything wrong.” </p><p>“To be met with violence is abnormal. entries.title: Cubs clinch postseason spot, celebrate and see what’s possible: ‘We’re built for the weird [stuff]’
entries.summary: <p>As the champagne flowed in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ clubhouse after they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/24/cubs-clinch-postseason-marlins-wild-card-seeding-still-a-mystery" >clinched a spot in the postseason</a> Thursday, a small circle of players was interested in a different beverage.</p><p>And interested in what’s next.</p><p>“Cold beers and World Series!” someone shouted before a ceremonial shotgunning.</p><p>Will there be another one of these soaking-wet celebrations at the end of October?</p><p>That’s what’s next, finding out how far into the playoffs — which start, somewhere, with an opening-round, best-of-three series Tuesday — this Cubs team can go.</p><p>“It’s all about what’s next,” said starting pitcher Matthew Boyd, who tossed seven innings of one-run ball in a 2-1 win over the Marlins. “It’s acknowledging this year and everything that’s happened and acknowledging, at the same time, going, ‘OK, cool. There’s a lot still to be done.’</p><p>“We want to host games at Wrigley. We’ve got to take care of our business. After that, comes the challenge of the postseason. It’s welcomed, it’s exciting, it’s why you play this game, for moments like this, for moments that are coming up.”</p><p>What’s coming up, in the immediate, is a weather-impacted three-game series against the Red Sox in Boston. There’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-red-sox-friday-doubleheader-boston-weather-forecast-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-playoffs-postseason" >an unusual doubleheader</a> Friday that will foist pitching questions upon the Cubs as they attempt to not only lock down home-field advantage in the first round but align their arms for that series.</p><p>Their opponents and the location of the games? To be determined.</p><p>They started Thursday tied for second in the wild-card standings with the Phillies, both teams a game behind the first-place Padres. The Cubs would host a first-round series if they finished atop those wild-card standings. Finishing second or third would send them elsewhere.</p><p>But the Cubs believe they’re well equipped for the uncertainty to come, this weekend and beyond, after dealing with obstacles all season, be that their on-field play — the team had a pair of 10-game win streaks early and a 10-game losing streak later on — or a midsummer avalanche of pitching injuries that threatened to bury them.</p><p>Every team deals with injuries, sure. But at one point, the Cubs had an entire rotation and late-inning relief group on the injured list at the same time.</p><p>They survived, still waking up Thursday with the best offense and best defense in baseball. They went to bed Thursday having officially obtained a playoff spot.</p><p>“We have taken a lot of hits this year,” said center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong on the day he clinched the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/24/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-40-40-season-baseball-history-mvp-home-runs-stolen-bases" >seventh 40-40 season</a> in baseball history. “We’ve still found ourselves here.</p><p>“We’re weathered. We’re going to be better for that, too. We know it’s not going to be easy, ever. Getting to go through a bunch of weird stuff and injuries and weird injuries, we’re built for the weird s--t.”</p><p>As tested as this team has been, its biggest tests still await. And truth be told, these were the tests these Cubs were waiting for.</p><p>They set championship-level goals in the spring and have been chasing them all season. Jed Hoyer’s front office was aggressive last offseason, trading for starting pitcher Edward Cabrera and signing third baseman Alex Bregman. It got aggressive again at the trade deadline, making win-now moves for pitchers Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes.</p><p>At times, along the way, these Cubs have looked perfectly capable of achieving those sky-high goals, at others, making everyone wonder how they could possibly hope to.</p><p>The highest-scoring offense in the sport mustered only six runs in three days against the sub-.500 Marlins.</p><p>Meanwhile, Bregman, their second best hitter, is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-alex-bregman-face-injury-return-matt-shaw-bunt-daniel-palencia-stats" >trying to come back from freak facial fractures</a> after taking a foul ball off his face last weekend. Gausman has spent two days <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-magic-number-playoffs-clinch-nl-wild-card-standings-kevin-gausman-shoulder-injury" >talking about a shoulder injury</a> after making a diving tag Wednesday.</p><p>But winning — and champagne showers — have a tendency of washing the worries away, at least temporarily, and sending the vibes swinging back in the anything-is-possible direction.</p><p>“Getting through 162 isn’t easy,” left fielder Ian Happ said. “You saw it with our team and the injuries we had to go through. You’ve got to celebrate the regular season and what it means. It’s just the beginning, but it’s a special thing.</p><p>“This group has a lot of belief in what’s to come over the next month.”</p>

entries.title: City to replace Northwest Side resident-built benches as advocates say more are on the way
entries.summary: <p>A pair of yellow and blue colored benches built by a local group to place at bus stops without pedestrian seating will be taken down by the city this week — and replaced with ones up to municipal code.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/14/cta-bus-stop-bench-ukrainian-village" target="_blank" ><u>two benches</u></a> — at Damen Avenue and Thomas Street, as well as Division Street and Oakley Boulevard — were placed without seeking permission from the city, said Sam Kovnar, 25, founder of the Northwest Neighborhood Alliance.</p><p>But they were enough to get the attention of the 1st Ward office, which told Kovnar the city was expected to be placing ones up to specifications at the bus stops, but offered to work with him to get more “decorative” benches down the line, according to emails reviewed by the Sun-Times. The current resident-made benches bear colors of the Ukrainian flag.</p><p>It was exactly what the group had hoped for in putting them there in the first place, Kovnar said. </p><p>“It’s very encouraging to have the support of the ward office,” Kovnar said. “We were worried the city would take them away and not replace them with anything. … We definitely want to build more. The question is how many and how soon?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4a0000" month.</p><p>A spokesperson for the 1st Ward said the office was “excited about the push for more benches to make our neighborhoods more accessible.”</p><p>“To have residents who care so much for their neighborhood is inspiring,” 1st Ward Ald. Daniel La Spata said in a statement. “Hopefully we can help them build on these efforts in 2027.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/14/cta-bus-stop-bench-ukrainian-village" >This group is building benches at bus stops that don’t have one. Will the city let them stay?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The Chicago Department of Transportation didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Kovnar said they haven’t heard if the benches will be returned to them, and expect them to be destroyed, though they are hesitant to remove them since they don’t have a timeline for when city-approved benches will replace them.</p><p>Going forward, though, Kovnar is hopeful the city will be willing to work with his “rag tag” group of bench designers to help identify places across the city where people are in need of a place to sit.</p><p>“We’d love to be able to work with [the city], since we’re already going through this the roundabout way,” Kovnar said. “This could be a lot easier if we had a direct dialogue with CDOT.”</p><p>The Chicago Transit Authority has almost 11,000 bus stops in Chicago, but many of them don’t have benches as part of a city push to deter loitering.</p><p>But benches play an important role in the community, Kovnar said. In addition to ensuring those waiting for buses — especially riders who are elderly or have disabilities — have a place to sit while they wait for buses, they can beautify an area and help residents feel more connected.</p><p>“It’s what makes a neighborhood feel like a place as opposed to a road,” Kovnar said. “Having a place to sit and make that comfortable, it can go a long way toward making the wait easier.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs marvel at Pete Crow-Armstrong’s 40-40 campaign: ‘One of the all-time seasons in baseball history’
entries.summary: <p>MVP resumes don’t get stronger than this.</p><p>“That’s the best year of baseball I’ve ever seen,” left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> said.</p><p><b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b>, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ superstar center fielder who’s seemingly had the MVP on lockdown for a couple months, did something Thursday that only six other players ever had accomplished, joining one of baseball’s most exclusive clubs by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/24/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-40-40-season-baseball-history-mvp-home-runs-stolen-bases" >stealing his 40th base</a> and securing a 40-homer, 40-steal season.</p><p>He can now count himself among this group: <b>Jose Canseco</b> (1988), <b>Barry Bonds</b> (1996), <b>Alex Rodriguez</b> (1998), <b>Alfonso Soriano</b> (2006), <b>Ronald Acuna Jr.</b> (2023) and <b>Shohei Ohtani</b> (2024).</p><p>It’s the cherry on top of what’s been a remarkable season for the 24-year-old, who has starred as the Cubs have chased championship-level goals.</p><p>Regardless of whether the Cubs take home a trophy at the end of October, Crow-Armstrong will need to clear room on his mantle.</p><p>“It’s one of those things where you’ve got to stop and pinch yourself and step back and go, ‘Man, we’re witnessing one of the all-time seasons in baseball history,’” starting pitcher <b>Matthew Boyd</b> said. “To get to [watch] it first-hand, you almost take it for granted, because you get to see the amazing stuff he’s doing on defense and offense every single night.”</p><p>But as Crow-Armstrong has spent the season doing unbelievable things, he’s spent it downplaying those things, too, instead choosing to prioritize team goals.</p><p>On the day he hit 40-40, he got to celebrate a team goal achieved, with the Cubs <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/24/cubs-clinch-mlb-postseason-playoffs-pete-crow-armstrong-matthew-boyd-nl-wild-card-standings-red-sox-doubleheader" >clinching a playoff spot</a> with a win over the Marlins.</p><p>He was repeatedly doused in champagne by teammates in the postgame celebration, happiest, on the doorstep of an MVP, that his huge numbers mean he helped his team win.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/46RrxUBZ2a4?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Pete Crow-Armstrong is doused by teammates after the Cubs clinched a playoff berth"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“If I could do that every year, then I would be a pretty content person at the end of my career,” he said. “Talking about how I’ve framed this year and how I wanted to achieve things, just approaching every day with winning in mind has gotten me here, and it started all these conversations about MVP and all that crap.”</p><p>Unsurprisingly, all Crow-Armstrong is thinking about is more wins.</p><p>That would mean more champagne. Hopefully he’s OK with that.</p><p>“It stung more this year than last year,” he said. “I have more cuts on my body. I was maybe a little more sunburnt for this.</p><p>“I might just be too fair-skinned for all the showers, because it stings.”</p><h3><b>Gausman in doubt for playoffs?</b></h3><p>Will righty <b>Kevin Gausman</b> be able to pitch in an opening-round playoff series?</p><p>The headlining acquisition in the front office’s trade-deadline haul wasn’t feeling good a day after he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-magic-number-playoffs-clinch-nl-wild-card-standings-kevin-gausman-shoulder-injury" >banged his left shoulder</a> while making a tag play at third base in Wednesday’s loss.</p><p>His comments Thursday didn’t do anything to assuage concerns that the Cubs could be without a critical piece of their rotation when the postseason begins Tuesday.</p><p>“Not great,” Gausman said when asked how he felt when he woke up. “I was pretty sore. I had a hard time sleeping.</p><p>“I’m pretty sore, but we’ll get some treatment today and take it day by day.”</p><p>Is there any doubt he’d be able to pitch next week?</p><p>“I don’t know,” he said. “I’m not going to make that judgment now. But I’ll do everything I can to be ready for whenever I’m asked to be ready. I can guarantee that.”</p><h3><b>Twin-bill starters</b></h3><p>There’s still much to play for in the Cubs’ final regular-season series against the Red Sox this weekend.</p><p>That set starts with a doubleheader Friday. Righty <b>Clay Holmes</b> and lefty <b>David Peterson</b> will start Games 1 and 2, respectively.</p>

entries.title: White Sox prioritizing rest, division race as they set final rotation order
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — As the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> plotted their rotation order for the end of the regular season, wildly divergent scenarios lay in front of them.</p><p>If they edge out the Guardians and win the American League Central, the Sox would almost certainly claim the No. 2 seed in the AL bracket, and have five days off between their regular-season finale and Game 1 of the ALDS. If the Sox stay in the third wild-card spot they clinched on Thursday, their first playoff game will be next Tuesday, and no one who starts this weekend against the Rockies would be rested enough to be an option for it.</p><p>Ultimately, manager <b>Will Venable </b>said playoff rotation ordering didn’t guide their thinking to pick <b>David Sandlin </b>to start Thursday in Kansas City, before having the top of their rotation in <b>Sean Burke</b>, <b>Davis Martin </b>and <b>Anthony Kay </b>finish out the season.</p><p>“We’re just not in a position to line guys up,” Venable said before Sandlin threw six innings of one-run ball in a 9-1 victory. “The division is very much in our sights too. We want to do everything we can to put our best foot forward.”</p><p>After Monday’s off day, the Sox could have pushed Burke up to start Thursday on regular rest, and be in line to pitch again in Game 1 of a wild-card series on Tuesday. But with Burke already at a professional career-high in innings, Martin battling right calf discomfort that shortened his last outing, and Kay six starts removed from the last time he completed five innings, Venable felt granting his starters an extra day of rest was more important.</p><p>“It gets to a point where you want to make sure that those guys are at their best when it matters the most, which is these four games,” Venable said.</p><p><b>Castillo sidelined</b></p><p>After getting booted from the rotation and yielding a grand slam in a low-leverage relief appearance on Tuesday, trade-deadline headliner <b>Luis Castillo </b>was -unlikely to have a role on a Sox playoff roster. That became all but official on Thursday, as the Sox placed Castillo on the injured list with right shoulder impingement. Reliever <b>Tyler Davis </b>was recalled from Triple-A Charlotte to fill Castillo’s spot and pitched a scoreless eighth inning.</p><p>Castillo has a 8.42 ERA in a Sox -uniform.</p><p><b>Martin: Calf not to blame</b></p><p>If Martin had his way, the right calf discomfort he has been managing since April would’ve been something he disclosed during a Sox World Series parade, with no one knowing he’d been playing through pain until the season was over.</p><p>Even now that he has stabilized things to the tune of an 0.89 ERA across four September outings, Martin isn’t inclined to blame his calf for the 7.06 ERA he ran from June through August.</p><p>“To be honest, it’s been getting back to being me, my personality, and that’s not an angry person,” Martin told the Sun-Times. “I was very angry because I was just mad at my results, mad at what was going on, and obviously you have mechanical issues on top of that.”</p><p>Simultaneously, Martin explains that maintaining an upright posture on the mound is critical for his command, and that unless his right arm falls off, he’s good to pitch.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: The first step to a busy offseason is for Sky principal owner Michael Alter to own up to mistakes
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON D.C — There’s no sense in sugarcoating it. This season represented a worst-case scenario for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a>, a cosmic repudiation of three years’ worth of offseason dealings. Their new face of the franchise, Rickea Jackson, acquired in a deal with the Sparks, tore her ACL four games into the season.</p><p>Their former face of the franchise, Angel Reese, traded to the Dream for late-round draft picks, solidified herself as a top-15 player in the league.</p><p>And Lynx rookie Olivia Miles, who the Sky could have drafted had they not traded up to get Reese, has surpassed everyone’s wildest expectations, looking like Lindsay Whalen and Maya Moore and Luka Doncic all rolled into one.</p><p>But wait, there’s more!</p><p>For all their troubles this season, their eleventh place finish, their fourth quarter collapses, there will be no consolation prize. The lottery pick that normally helps franchises to rebound — they owe that to the Mystics, the consequence of an impatient deal from 2024.</p><p>Accordingly, the Sky are heading into the offseason with some big questions.</p><p>Will they replace coach Tyler Marsh? How long does general manager Jeff Pagliocca have left? What are they going to do at the point guard position?</p><p>And, even more existentially: What is principal owner Michael Alter’s plan for getting the Sky to compete in a bigger, better WNBA?</p><p>Alter is now the league’s second-longest tenured owner, having founded the team in 2005. He’s had moments to brag about, including a championship in 2021. But in the last five years he has not responded swiftly and boldly enough to the league’s changing dynamics.</p><p>The WNBA has grown exponentially, both in the number of teams and the investment those teams make in infrastructure — read, practice facilities — and staff — read, front office.</p><p>That the Sky missed the first wave of teams building dedicated practice facilities, and that they’ve missed their own deadlines for the one under construction in Bedford Park, has been painfully obvious.</p><p>Less visible, but just as painful, is their lagging approach to building out their front office. It is still staffed by just one person: Pagliocca.</p><p>I wrote a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/09/11/sky-owner-michael-alter-should-reconsider-one-man-band-approach-to-front-office" >couple weeks ago</a> that Alter should put a math and strategy-minded team under him.</p><p>The Lynx are the obvious example for why; a sound projection in 2024 that the Sky would end up a lottery team ultimately netted them Miles. But my concern, at its core, extends beyond the size of the front office. It extends beyond the practice facility delays too.</p><p>Practice facilities and front offices have been progress points across the league in recent years, but the top teams will always be pushing the frontier. What's the next growth area? The Sky need to be able to anticipate it and get out in front of it.</p><p>I wish I had a 12-step process for how to get there. I don’t. What I do have is the first step — a simple one Alter can take in the coming weeks — which is to publicly address the fans and own up to mistakes.</p><p>If he needs a little inspiration, he can look across town to see how the Bulls did it. That organization has also stagnated in recent years, but as a part of their front office rebuild, owner <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/04/07/chicago-bulls-michael-reinsdorf-search-top-executive/" target="_blank" >Michael Reinsdorf acknowledged</a> that the organization has not done a great job of anticipating where the league is going. It’s a small admission, but it helps to build credibility and excitement around the team’s new direction.</p><p>Alter needs to do the same.</p><p>Regardless of what he decides about Marsh and Pagliocca's futures, it's time for him to come out and say: we’ve missed some things. And we don’t just have a plan for catching up, we’ve got a plan for being on the cutting edge.</p><p>That will require him to let go of the defensive posture that so many executives — especially Sky ones — use when speaking to the public.</p><p>Their communication around practice facility delays is just one example. Ownership said the facility would be ready ahead of this season, but it’s still not done. And as they’ve blown past two years’ worth of deadlines, they haven’t acknowledged a single mistake, maintaining that the delays are just due to weather or bad luck or a need to expand.</p><p>Being defensive has its roots in real dynamics. The Sky became the poster child online for a poorly-operated WNBA team, when organizations including the Sparks, Wings, Sun and others had many of the same issues.</p><p>Public conversation does lack nuance and isn’t always fair. But it can benefit from guidance. And if you can’t acknowledge your flaws, you can’t expect anyone to believe that you're going to change.</p><p>WNBA fans now more than ever want to be informed and engaged. That’s what makes the women’s basketball boom so special, and it’s especially true in Chicago. These fans are locked in and loyal.</p><p>The scene at Wintrust Arena shows it. You would’ve thought that with Reese gone and the wins still few and far between, the place would be a ghost town. But fans have stuck with it — attendance is down less than 10% from 2025.</p><p>I couldn’t believe how many people showed up for the final home game earlier this week, a meaningless skirmish between the Sky and Tempo’s JV teams. The stadium was eighty-percent full, and when veteran guard Elizabeth Williams took the mic to thank them for their support, everyone was on their feet, applauding.</p><p>The fans really want this. They’re ready to get behind something sustainable.</p><p>Imagine what it would bring to the league to have one of its oldest franchises and biggest markets thriving and leading the way.</p><p>Acknowledging mistakes shouldn’t preclude Alter from being proud of meaningful progress this season. Beating the Aces and Valkyries at home, taking the Fever to overtime on the road — none of that happens by accident. They’ve assembled some real pieces in Sydney Taylor, Kamilla Cardoso and Gabriela Jaquez, not to mention the injured Jackson. </p><p>But he needs to be sober and humble about what’s left to prove. This young core still lacks the track-record of playoff-bound ones on the Mystics, Fever, and Wings — or even rebuilding teams like the Storm.</p><p>And even if they do prove themselves as playoff-level pillars: why should fans believe that they’ll commit to Chicago long-term?</p><p>Why should they believe that the front office will make the right moves around them?</p><p>A little humility from Alter would go a long way right now.</p><p>Maybe all this is giving him too much credit. Maybe his sincerity will mean nothing because he is simply not wealthy or sophisticated enough to finance the necessary investments to keep pace in a booming league. If that’s true, he should sell the team.</p><p>But since he was capable of scrapping together $60 million of financing for the practice facility, according to the team, I’m not so sure money is the only thing holding the Sky back.</p><p>I think humility and vulnerable communication are part of it too.</p><p>That’s the first step. If you're reading this, Mr. Alter, it's time to hop to it.</p>

entries.title: Catholic leaders and advocates honor those killed in ICE custody, push for immigrant protections
entries.summary: <p>Armed with 104 crosses, each adorned with an individual name, Catholic leaders and union workers united at a downtown church Thursday to introduce a new installation meant to honor victims of aggressive immigration practices and push for reform.</p><p>The installation memorializes each person who has died in immigration custody or during immigration operations since 2020 by painting their names on a cross. The crosses will be displayed at Holy Name Cathedral on the Near North Side and moved to different parishes in the Chicago area, including Catholic Theological Union in Hyde Park and St. Sabina in Auburn Gresham.</p><p>The Rev. Brendan Curran, co-founder of Priests for Justice for Immigrants, said the project is two-fold: to honor those who have died and work toward better treatment of immigrants, including supporting political candidates who support immigrant rights.</p><p>“This side of this exhibit is a very clear indication that our system is broken, and we have to do something better than this for the future of this country,” Curran said.</p><p>He encouraged Catholics and others who are immigrant advocates to vote in the November midterm elections and put pressure on members of Congress to restore Temporary Protected Status for Haitian immigrants. Curran also urged support for the Drain ICE Act, a bill introduced in February that would pull $75 billion in funding from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other federal immigration enforcement systems.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-050000" name="image-050000"></a> <picture entries.title: Bulls Prep's young defense grows up in win against Lincoln Park
entries.summary: <p>Bulls Prep coach Michael Willis says his defensive backfield has been shaky this season. His team has leaned on an experienced line that competed in a Class 5A state playoff game last season.</p><p>The young defense is starting to grow up. Juniors Tyran Jenkins and Ezran Johnson both returned interceptions for touchdowns in Bulls Prep’s 30-10 win against Lincoln Park on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/24/high-school-football-scores-week-6" >Thursday</a> at Lane Stadium.</p><p>“I zoned out after I caught it and then celebrated with my teammates on the sidelines,” Jenkins said.</p><p>Lincoln Park (3-3, 1-2 Red Shield) led 7-6 after Stephen Akwfo connected with Anthony Jennings for an 11-yard touchdown just before halftime.</p><p>Bulls Prep’s defense dominated the second half. The Lions finished with just 46 rushing yards and 73 passing yards.</p><p>“We have a lot of seniors and some good leadership,” Willis said. “They understand they need to lift their brothers up and be positive.”</p><p>Quarterback Zylin Lewis scored on an 11-yard run with 8:23 left in the third quarter to put Bulls Prep ahead for good.</p><p>“It was just me following my linemen,” Lewis said. “My brothers set up the play for me. I knew that we had to get the score to win the game and bring it back home to the West Side for our families.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: 3 wounded in South Chicago drive-by shooting
entries.summary: <p>Three people were shot in South Chicago Thursday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The victims were standing in the 8700 block of South Commercial Avenue at 8 p.m. when a passenger in a silver SUV fired shots before the vehicle fled eastbound on 87th Street, police said. </p><p>A 32-year-old man was wounded in the left shin, a 49-year-old man was shot in his right calf, and a 38-year-old man was hit in the cheek and neck, police said. All three were taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in fair condition.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said. </p>

entries.title: Man gets probation for throwing liquid at teens, parents at Avondale Mexican dance studio
entries.summary: <p>A man pleaded guilty to misdemeanor battery charges for throwing a bucket of liquid onto teens and parents at a Northwest Side Mexican dance studio, according to court records.</p><p>Robert Villanueva, 50, was sentenced to six months of probation after he pleaded guilty to five counts of misdemeanor battery Wednesday, according to Cook County court records. He was originally <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/11/man-charged-with-tossing-liquid-on-mexican-dance-studio-students-in-avondale" target="_blank" ><u>charged</u></a> in the incident in March.</p><p>A video of the incident posted to social media shows Villanueva and a woman, who wasn’t charged, on a fire escape shouting, “You’re lucky ICE is not here.” Villanueva then throws cups of liquid toward the group, which was leaving Ballet Folklorico, a traditional Mexican folk dance studio in Avondale.</p><p>Earlier this year, Chicago police said the victims were a boy, 13, three girls — ages 13, 14 and 15 — and three women — ages 43, 41 and 40. At the time, police said there were other victims at the scene not listed in the report.</p><p>Villanueva’s probation will end in March, just weeks after the anniversary of the incident.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/11/man-charged-with-tossing-liquid-on-mexican-dance-studio-students-in-avondale" >Man charged with tossing liquid on Mexican dance studio students in Avondale</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Semi catches fire in rollover crash near Chicago Skyway
entries.summary: <p>No one was injured after a semitruck hit a tree, rolled over and caught fire on Interstate 90 Thursday night, according to the Chicago fire and police departments.</p><p>Around 8:47 p.m., firefighters responded to the scene of a semitruck that rolled after it hit a tree along an I-90 exit ramp near State Street. Fuel from the vehicle then caught fire in the roadway, fire officials said. No injuries were reported. </p><p>Firefighters at the scene requested sand to absorb flammable liquids that leaked from the vehicle, fire officials said. The accident is under investigation.</p>

entries.title: Man and woman fatally shot in Austin; 'known' shooter in custody
entries.summary: <p>Charges are pending for a suspect who police said opened fire at a man and a woman he knows, killing them Thursday night inside an Austin home. </p><p>Around 10:45 p.m., a witness heard gunshots coming from the basement of a home in the 800 block of North Parkside Avenue and called 911, Chicago police said. </p><p>A 47-year-old woman was shot in the chest and a 27-year-old man was shot in the body, according to police. Both were taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where they died. </p><p>Two guns were found at the scene and the shooter was placed in custody. </p><p>Area 4 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: Not in Kansas — as we know it — anymore
entries.summary: <p>The home of Dwight Eisenhower and Amelia Earhart is rarely part of the national conversation — but that could be about to change. It is becoming clear that the race for Senate this year could be a huge upset. In the 19th century, Kansas was the scene of violent clashes over slavery, which temporarily earned it the moniker "bleeding Kansas," and in the 20th it was the birthplace of Brown v. Board of Education, one of the most consequential Supreme Court cases in American history. </p><p>But in recent decades, it's been a backwater, mostly due to its size (a bit under 3 million people) and political lopsidedness. Kansas has gone red in every presidential contest since 1968 and hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.</p><p>In light of that history, it would be foolish to get one's hopes up too much about the Senate contest there this year. After all, the Republican incumbent, Roger Marshall, won his 2020 race by more than 11 points. But he isn't sounding confident. At a recent debate, he bellowed over boos from the crowd, "What you're going to get from me — you may not agree with me on everything — but you're going to know exactly where I stand." That sounds like someone who feels trapped and is making a virtue of necessity.</p><p>Marshall is trapped. Like nearly all Republicans, he has lashed himself to Donald Trump as Odysseus bound himself to the ship's mast. He has bowed and scraped to MAGA with the best of them, even going so far as to praise Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s cracked Make America Healthy Again agenda while measles deaths mount — and now he cannot escape.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f00000" name="module-f00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Midterm elections are nearly always referenda on the sitting president. You can track the out party's likely performance by knowing the popularity of the incumbent president. Though Kansans have a higher opinion of Trump than most of the country, his standing in the state has eroded. At the start of his second term, 60% of Kansans had a favorable opinion of Trump. Today, only 47% do. Among independents, 59% disapprove.</p><p>Like the rest of the country, Kansas has been burdened by high costs, but it's been particularly hard hit by Trump's trade and immigration policies. A Wichita State professor of international business estimates that Kansas is one of the most trade-dependent states in the country. One in six jobs in the state is directly tied to exports. Some tariffs might temporarily boost prices for some domestic products, like beef (which helps ranchers), but the chaotic implementation of the tariffs vitiated even that scant benefit. After imposing tariffs on imported beef, Trump repeatedly withdrew or weakened them, only to announce in August that the United States would suspend quotas on up to 660 million pounds of imported ground beef in an effort to reduce prices at the supermarket. As Americans have fully digested by now, tariffs are taxes that raise the prices of things we buy.</p><p>Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, whose last foray into helping consumers was a recommendation that we all raise chickens in our backyards, seems unwilling to acknowledge the inevitable conflict between pandering to producers and pandering to consumers. She announced that the new policy would "protect the American rancher" and "the American consumer." This was tough for both of Kansas' Republican senators to swallow (as it were). Marshall said he was "frustrated" by the president's actions, while Terry Moran, apparently asleep for the past 10 years as Trump has flattened every laissez-faire principle imaginable, urged the president to "let the free market work."</p><p>Kansas' beef with the administration goes beyond cattle. Kansas is the largest wheat-producing state in the union, and the twin blows of record-high diesel fuel prices and rising costs of fertilizer due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have been painful. This year, farmers are in doubt about how much to plant as export markets have been thrown into turmoil by Trump's trade wars. Marshall bleats wanly that "the tariffs are working," but tariffs on steel and aluminum have damaged the state's large aviation industry, and as one small business owner observed sourly, her fertilizer bill had tripled this year and her diesel bill had doubled.</p><p>One of Kansas' largest employers is the Canadian aviation firm Bombardier, which employs more than 1,500 people (and 2,000 more in other states). While slapping Canada around, Trump has name-checked Bombardier, saying their products are not "good enough" and threatening to ban sales of their products in the United States. (If their products are so bad, why are people willingly buying them?) Employees at one of Bombardier's Wichita plants were rattled. One told a Washington Post reporter, "This is ridiculous. We have thousands of Americans working here." The Post delicately added that the employee used a profanity. Kansas' two Republican senators are looking at their shoes and kicking sand, though Marshall did post that "I'm going to fight to keep Bombardier's over 1,200 Kansas jobs. I've already taken that concern inside the Oval Office."</p><p>How reassuring that must be.</p><h3>Appropriate challenger</h3><p>Here's another reason Marshall has cause to feel trapped: The Democrats have chosen a fantastically appropriate challenger. No DSA-adjacent progressive here. Instead, they nominated Adam Hamilton, pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, the largest Methodist congregation in the U.S.</p><p>Hamilton is an articulate moderate, author of 30 books, who agrees that the border was out of control under Joe Biden but notes that the indiscriminate meat cleaver approach to immigration enforcement under Trump is damaging both economically and morally. "So right now, when you travel to southeast, southwest Kansas, you're talking to people in the meatpacking industry, the cattle industry, and they're saying, 'Forty percent of our workforce are immigrants, and we need them, and we care about them.'" Later, he continued, "Stop demonizing them. Figure out a plan to bring immigrants in where it's legal for them to be here, and where we can welcome them instead of (them) having to live in fear in our businesses or our communities."</p><p>Hamilton's statistics are accurate, or perhaps a bit understated. Without those immigrant employees at meat processing facilities, prices of meat will climb even higher, to say nothing of the cruelty of uprooting families with long ties to the community and no criminal offenses of any kind.</p><p>Hamilton calls Trump's tariffs "a disaster for everyone across the state of Kansas," and hits the corruption theme hard. That's exactly the kind of Democrat a Republican state demands.</p><p>Kansas is red, it's true. But it has often chosen Democrats for governor, including incumbent Laura Kelly. So it isn't as if Kansans' fingers just can't check off a Democratic box. After Hamilton won the primary, the Cook Political Report moved the race from "solid" to "likely" Republican. It is probably still Marshall's race to lose, but the tailwind for Hamilton reflects just how badly Trump has betrayed his own base as well as the opportunities that open up when a) there's a wave building, and b) the nominee matches the constituency.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-590000" name="module-590000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Jurors need clarity when considering fates of mentally ill defendants
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/jurors-speak-out-about-lindsay-clancy-mistrial-and-the-lone-holdout" target="_blank" >mistrial</a> in the Lindsay Clancy case highlights a truth Illinois should confront. Clancy’s Massachusetts jurors understood that a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity would not mean freedom; it would mean commitment to a psychiatric hospital, with any release subject to continuing judicial review.</p><p>Illinois does not provide jurors with comparable candor regarding its guilty but mentally ill verdict. The label sounds like a humane compromise — guilt accompanied by guaranteed treatment. It is not.</p><p>Under Illinois law, a person found guilty but mentally ill receives precisely the same sentence as any other person convicted of the offense and is sent directly to the Illinois Department of Corrections. The statute promises only whatever treatment the IDOC itself determines is necessary, guaranteeing neither hospitalization nor a higher level of care than what is available to the general prison population.</p><p>That distinction is not academic. The recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/24/joliet-prison-fires-mental-health-illinois-department-corrections" >investigation</a> by The Marshall Project, WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times on the Joliet Treatment Center — the prison intended to provide intensive mental healthcare — documented more than 70 fires in three years, including repeated acts of self-immolation and two deaths.</p><p>Perhaps most tellingly, the IDOC’s own annual report does not separately track individuals sentenced as guilty but mentally ill. Illinois cannot evaluate whether the verdict fulfills its promise if the state does not publicly account for those receiving it.</p><p>Jurors should be told plainly that not guilty by reason of insanity verdicts can lead to secure hospitalization, while guilty but mentally ill ordinarily leads to prison. Illinois should require a complete consequences instruction for juries, and either create a meaningful treatment pathway for guilty but mentally ill defendants or abolish a verdict that promises care in name only.</p><p><i>Attorney Kulmeet “Bob” Galhotra, </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/12/31/21044574/head-cook-county-public-defenders-homicide-task-force-retires-kulmeet-bob-galhotra" ><i>former supervisor, Cook County Public Defender’s Homicide Task Force</i></a><i>, Galewood</i> </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e50000" name="module-e50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>More UN delegates should have walked out on Trump</h3><p>On Tuesday while addressing the United Nations General Assembly, President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/trump-address-united-nations-general-assembly-iran-war-rcna599085" target="_blank" >said</a> that he could “annihilate the Islamic Republic" and "drive them into hell with no chance of survival,” at which point the Iranian delegation walked out. (The U.S. delegation did the <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jnXv_QNqX7A" target="_blank" >same</a> the next day during the Iranian president's U.N. speech)</p><p>What a magnificent moment it would've been had the entire standing-room-only audience of global representatives had done the same when Trump spoke, sending a clear message to the reckless out-of-control maniac who tragically holds America’s highest office.</p><p><i>Rob Hirsh, West Ridge</i></p><h3>Bears don’t need to leave Soldier Field</h3><p>According to Wikipedia, Soldier Field has a seating capacity of <a class="Link" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soldier_Field" target="_blank" >62,500 people</a> for football games. However, the attendance for Sunday's game against the Vikings was only <a class="Link" href="https://www.espn.com/nfl/recap/_/gameId/401872937" target="_blank" >58,914</a>. </p><p>One wonders why an organization that can't fill one of the smallest stadiums in the NFL for its home opener thinks it deserves public support for a new stadium. So many critical needs are currently inadequately supported or going unmet. The McCaskeys' Bears should be told to move to the back of the line.</p><p><i>Chet Alexander, Alsip</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Self-centered grandmother alienates entire family
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a mother-in-law of 30 years I distance myself from. I do this in order to maintain my sanity. She seems incapable of carrying on a normal conversation and responds to any comment or question by talking about herself, even though it usually has nothing to do with what was said. What bothers me most is when she's around our adult children. She won't ask them any questions, isn't interested in how they are or what they are up to, and doesn't say anything loving or kind. Instead, she drones on about other people in her life who have nothing to do with us. We constantly say we don't know that person, but she continues talking about them. I have tried for many years to redirect conversations, to no avail.</p><p>She has been this way for as long as I have known her. Do you think it's possible to get through to a person like this, to make her understand how a normal conversation should go? Do you think it's terrible for her grandchildren not to want to be around her? I don't encourage them to spend much time with her because they end up feeling annoyed and disappointed. That, however, does not sit well with their father. Any thoughts would be appreciated. — <i>FRUSTRATED DAUGHTER-IN-LAW</i></p><p><b>DEAR FRUSTRATED:</b> Your mother-in-law appears to be solely centered upon herself. If, after 30 years, you haven't been able to get through to her that her lack of interest in her grandchildren has isolated her from them, you and your husband must recognize that she isn't going to change. There is no quick fix for this. After three decades of this treatment, your children will never want to be in their grandmother's presence any more than they are required to be, whether it sits well with their father or not.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My sister and I have an OK relationship. When we were younger, we always fought, but that's what siblings do. When my father died, I learned about it not from a phone call, but on social media. To say I was hurt and angry is an understatement.</p><p>How can I get past this? I told my sister how hurt I was when it happened, but I can't seem to move on. Now my mother is not doing well, and I'm afraid this will happen again since I have been named executor of her will and a trustee of any assets to be received by my older sister. What are your thoughts on how to get past this and potentially handle any future dealings? — <i>YOUNG EXECUTOR</i></p><p><b>DEAR YOUNG EXECUTOR:</b> I'm sorry to learn your mother is unwell. Executorship is a big responsibility. As you navigate the next steps, try to set the tone with humility. Instead of dwelling on the past, fulfill your duties objectively and with diligence. If the estate is large and your sister is unhappy with the terms of the will, consult a probate lawyer to keep matters from getting personal.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: It’s now nearly impossible to get asylum in Chicago immigration court
entries.summary: <p>The Venezuelan man believed his case for asylum checked all the boxes to let him stay in the United States.</p><p>He had proof of how badly local police hurt him when they kidnapped and sodomized him, the nadir of<b> </b>months of harassment. As a gay man, he’s considered part of a protected class. And after he reported the assaults, the officers swore revenge.</p><p>“They will kill me, these police officers,” he testified in Spanish in August. “They'll know when I am there” in Venezuela. “I don’t want to return.”</p><p>And yet, the federal immigration judge assigned to hear his case in downtown Chicago was not convinced. Among the doubts he cited in denying the case: he couldn’t believe that the two officers piled onto a single motorcycle with their victim. He said the documents lacked crucial details, and ultimately determined that the police, though in uniform, were acting on a personal grudge rather than official actions.</p><p>Judge Matthew C. Beese, a first of many<b> </b>hires to Chicago’s immigration court during President Donald Trump’s second term, has one of the lowest asylum approval rates in Chicago now, contributing to a larger trend nationally of plummeting rates.</p><p>In Chicago, the asylum approval rate is just 3.3% so far this year; last year it was 14.6%. The national average dropped to 2.1%, down from 8.8%, according to a Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ analysis of immigration court court data.</p><p>Asylum is historically a hard-won way<b> </b>to stay in the United States, requiring evidence of persecution back home that specifically targets protected groups of people, such as political dissidents or ethnic minorities. Escaping general dire conditions such as poverty, violence or a failing government was never sufficient to win asylum protection.</p><p>Since January 2025, when the newly inaugurated president immediately began ramping up deportations and removing millions of immigrants, his Department of Justice has<b> </b>foisted<b> </b>a major shake-up onto the immigration court it oversees. Veteran judges with deep backgrounds as immigration lawyers have been pushed out and replaced by new hires. A national social media campaign to recruit new judges continues to frame the role as a “deportation judge.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Department of Justice, which oversees immigration court and immigration judges, continues to advertise openings to become a “deportation judge” on its website.</p></figcaption></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In Chicago, many of the recent hires used to work in military and administrative law, rather than immigration law, and as such, they’re taking the bench largely without important context about the home countries immigrants have fled.</p><p>Immigration judges have also been saddled with heavy caseloads, narrowed rules aimed at granting fewer asylum cases, and a new urgency coming from Washington to wrap up cases for migrants from certain countries, lawyers and recently ousted judges say.</p><p>They also worry that due process in Chicago’s immigration court is slipping away.</p><p>“When people talk about justice in our immigration system, I think the important piece is whether someone has had their day in court,” says Eva Saltzman, one of the most recently fired judges, “and I think whether individuals receive due process is a reflection of the integrity of the judge and the integrity of the government overall.”</p><p>Asked for an interview, the Department of Justice instead sent a prepared statement from its press office declining to comment on personnel matters.</p><p>"Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration. The Justice Department is restoring integrity to our immigration system by hearing cases fairly, expeditiously, and uniformly, in accordance with the law,” it read.</p><p>“This Department of Justice continues to bring on talented legal professionals who are committed to protecting national security and public safety.”</p><h3> No background in immigration law</h3><p>Chicago’s immigration judges have seen a revolving door during the second Trump administration. Amid a flurry of changes by the Justice Department,<b> </b>a few experienced judges accepted early retirement<b> </b>or resigned, but at least six<b> </b>more in the court of about 20 have been fired without explanation, they say.</p><p>And for seven of the 10 judges newly appointed to hear cases in Chicago, their promotion appears to mark the start of their practice in immigration law.</p><p>A review of public records shows this holds true for Judge Beese, the Venezuelan man’s judge, who was appointed last October. Though a seasoned attorney licensed since 2003, Judge Beese’s Justice Department bio shows his seven years as a judge were spent as a municipal judge first in an Oklahoma town of about 500 and then as an administrative law judge for Oklahoma’s state regulatory commission governing utilities and oil and gas.</p><p>As a lawyer, he was a longtime deputy city attorney for Muskogee, Oklahoma, and had practiced family, criminal and general law around Rockford, Illinois.</p><p>Other new hires came from careers as military judges and as prosecutors. The three that have a background in immigration have worked for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.</p><p>Jennifer Peyton, Chicago’s former assistant chief of immigration court until she was fired in July 2025, says she’s found herself explaining facets of immigration law to some of the new judges now that she’s representing immigrants again in private practice.</p><p>She says she's had hearings with some of the newer judges, including ones in Chicago, where they've said things that run counter to immigration law. "And I'm like, 'that's impossible because of the posture of this case, like that can't happen,'" Peyton says. “I was lucky because I focused my entire career on immigration, so I had a pretty good grasp of [immigration law] going in.”</p><p>The new judges hired since 2025 in particular are driving down the asylum approval rate. Of the 1,638 asylum cases brought before them through August, they’ve granted just 25. That’s a 1.5% approval rating.</p><p>Beese, for example, has granted just 13 cases of the 802 that have come before him, and denied 212. He has ruled 511 of them “abandoned” — which could mean the immigrant didn’t show up in court or didn’t complete requirements such as being fingerprinted or submitting evidence, setting them on a path to deportation.<b> </b></p><p>Two of his new colleagues with more than 500 asylum rulings between them since their May appointments have yet to grant any asylum petitions at all. According to their Department of Justice biographies, both were former prosecutors and ICE lawyers, Shawn J. Abraham for six months in Chicago and Jaime Poarch for seven in Texas.</p><p>The Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis used data published by the Executive Office for Immigration Review, the government’s name for the immigration court<b>, </b>as collected by the Deportation Data Project, through the end of August.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-a90000" name="html-embed-module-a90000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30346340"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30346340/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-670000" name="html-embed-module-670000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-sankey" data-src="visualisation/30355932"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30355932/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="sankey visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3></h3><h3>Lots of rule changes, lots of firings</h3><p>Saltzman was one of the two judges fired in July, as asylum cases in Chicago peaked. One Thursday afternoon, as she was hearing cases, she says a brief email landed in her inbox telling her she was done. An immigration judge since 2016 with positive performance reviews, she was assigned to cases for immigrants in detention centers.</p><p>She also suspects her appointment by the Obama administration was a motive for her firing,<b> </b>saying in an interview,<b> </b>“I have seen that those not appointed by this administration were more quickly terminated.”</p><div class="Enhancement" where it appeared clear that that individual had established their eligibility for asylum under the current cases that have been published by the Board of Immigration Appeals, that individual is no longer eligible for asylum, and so I did find myself in accordance with the law deciding cases very differently than I may have two or three years ago.”</p><p>In late June, Judge Elizabeth Treacy
