here's the number of cases; these must be heard by X date, must be completed by this date,' without an explanation as to why.” Somalis, for example, who’ve been repeatedly vilified by the president, suddenly had their hearing dates moved up, cutting their time to gather evidence.</p><p>The changes felt wrong for Treacy, who had worked on the enforcement side of immigration, as a lawyer for ICE in class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Veteran immigration lawyer Andrew Sidea also has watched changes that sounded positive play out.</p><p>That included prioritizing families seeking asylum, which ended up curtailing the time clients of his — indigenous Bolivian political dissidents — needed to gather evidence from home. Their petition was denied in July.</p><p>He’s seen judicial discretion get tightened, tying judges’ hands. And overall, asylum seekers from several Central and South American countries — such as Venezuela, Honduras and Nicaragua —now face only a small chance of having their applications approved.</p><p>"If you really wanted to sort of see, what does it mean to be an immigration judge in the second President Trump era, any of the judges that have been there for a year or less will give you a very good idea as to what the judges are being told and trained by the Department of Justice," Sidea says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-070000" name="html-embed-module-070000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-scatter" data-src="visualisation/30347671"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30347671/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="scatter visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Saltzman sees patterns that mimic trends in the federal government.</p><p>Women have been “fired or terminated without cause in the Chicago immigration court since this administration began,” Saltzman says. “There have been during that time frame no male judges terminated. There were, I believe, the hiring of two new male judges announced the day before two of us female judges were terminated. So that is what it is.”</p><p>Currently, the Chicago court lists 20 judges, including an assistant chief and backup assistant chief; 14 of them are men. In January 2025, the reverse was true. Of 22 listed then, 14 were women.</p><h3></h3><h3>Due process under threat</h3><p>The churn has immigration court veterans worried that<b> </b>the judges’ ability to work independently has been under threat.</p><p>That puts due process for immigrants at risk too, Treacy says.</p><p>“I have worked under many different administrations, both Republican and Democrat, some are more enforcement minded, others are not,” she says, “but it always felt until now that there was some fairness, some order to what was happening, that that we were still operating within a fair system that honored due process.”</p><p>Peyton, Treacy’s former boss, is blunter, calling what’s happening, “intentional destructive acts of our administration towards the immigration courts, towards due process, and against the non-citizens.</p><p>“I'm seeing it as like a mass catastrophe against due process, finding procedural reasons to not have hearings where someone fears torture if they're going to go back to their home country,” says Peyton, once Chicago’s assistant chief of immigration court. </p><p>“I wish that people recognize that valid claims are being set aside every day for procedural roadblocks, and that has happened so much since January 20th [2025]. And I don't know if we're ever gonna get it back.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Chicago teens want more jobs and businesses in their neighborhoods, survey shows
entries.summary: <p>Chicago teens would like to see more investment in job opportunities and businesses on the South and West sides, according to a survey conducted by <a class="Link" href="https://www.formyblock.org/" target="_blank" >My Block, My Hood, My City</a> this summer.</p><p>The youth empowerment nonprofit collected responses in July during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/11/my-block-my-hood-my-city-downtown-day-teen-takeovers" target="_blank" ><u>Downtown Day</u></a>, an annual initiative that brings 1,000 teens into the city for a day of experiences that they select. Each participant was given a $50 prepaid debit card to use at destinations of their choice, which included the Art Institute of Chicago, Navy Pier, Shedd Aquarium, Water Tower Place and dozens more.</p><p>Teens were also asked how and where they would invest $50,000 — mirroring the collective sum of their gift cards — by placing push pins on a map of Chicago during the event. Of the 121 survey respondents, nearly 20% chose jobs as a priority, while about 15% chose businesses and retail. About 47% of the teens chose South Side community areas for all types of investment, while nearly 35% targeted the West Side.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The feedback will help My Block, My Hood, My City inform programming as the city grapples with how to make public spaces welcoming for young people while responding to concerns about large <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/moment-of-youth/2026/09/10/teen-beach-gathering-conflict" >teen gatherings</a> that can sometimes turn violent.</p><p>The data underscores that young people want to work and socialize where they live, but are contending with a lack of options in disinvested neighborhoods, the organization said.</p><p>“They want to be contributors in the city, and they want to be valued and looked at as an asset,” said Briana Mathews, manager of youth development at My Block, My Hood My City. “They want to be active in our city's ecosystem.”</p><h3>What Chicago teens want to see</h3><p>As part of the survey, teens were asked to select from eight categories for investment: educational programs, recreational spaces, mental health resources, jobs, parks and outdoor spaces, restaurants, housing and businesses and retail.</p><p>While jobs and businesses and retail garnered the most responses, the third-most popular choice was a tie between educational programs, housing and mental health resources.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-de0000" name="html-embed-module-de0000"></a><div style="min-height:379px" id="datawrapper-vis-sh34s"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/sh34s/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-sh34s"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/sh34s/full.png" alt="What and where teens would invest $50,000 in (Stacked Bars)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Downtown Day participant Del’Reona Cox, 16, said she would choose to invest the money in recreational spaces in her neighborhood, West Englewood. She envisions a place where people can listen to music, play basketball, draw: anything to keep people engaged and help them “find their crowds.”</p><p>“It would be to create a safe space for the teenagers – and maybe the older people – whose heads are not in the right places,” she said. “Like a reset to the mind. A fresh start.”</p><p>The neighborhood’s Ogden Park was approved for a new, <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2025/november/ogden-park-fieldhouse-announcement.html" target="_blank" ><u>$25 million fieldhouse</u></a> in 2025, but further details have not been announced. In the meantime, the park has been the site of teen gatherings, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/teen-takeover-green-line-l-terminal-chicago-englewood-community/" target="_blank" ><u>including one in July</u></a> that left some teens in police custody.</p><p>“I don’t go outside because of the teen takeovers,” Cox said. “It’s just not safe.”</p><p>Cox said police involvement has not helped to curb the gatherings either.</p><p>“They try to shut the parties down, but they just move it [to another location],” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" Englewood. “It would be to create a safe space for the teenagers – and maybe the older people – whose heads are not in the right places,” she said. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The ACE Amandla Charter High School student said she understands why many of her peers said they would invest in employment. She earns money by doing hair, and some young people in her neighborhood work at the park or McDonald’s.</p><p>But there is a need for more jobs, especially year-round, she said.</p><p>And she wasn’t surprised by the survey respondents who selected housing<b>. </b></p><p>“There's a lot of abandoned houses and vacant lots that can be filled in for things,” she said.</p><p>She also agreed with those concerned about mental health resources, given the mindset of some in her neighborhood.</p><p>“They live based on Instagram,” she said. “Maybe they didn't have the right resources and opportunities. Maybe somebody didn’t come in with open arms and redirect them.”</p><h3>A need for stability</h3><p>The city has made strides to employ teens through its <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoyouthworks.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Youth Works</u></a> initiative, which created more than 32,500 jobs this summer, <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/ChicagosMayor/status/2095527234568179727" target="_blank" ><u>according to Mayor Brandon Johnson</u></a>. Still, there is a demand for jobs that don’t require extensive transportation, Mathews said.</p><p>“I think they're talking about jobs that they can walk to,” she said of the survey respondents. “That they can leave high school and then walk to Panera Bread or Chipotle — being able to see institutions in their neighborhood.”</p><p>Being successful in the workplace also requires stability, Mathews said, so it makes sense that teens are asking for more investment in educational programs, housing and mental health resources.</p><p>“I think that they recognize that those tools are important to be able to participate [in the economy],” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Suburban man described as 'enforcer' for biker club is sentenced for broad-daylight beating of motorist
entries.summary: <p>It was like a scene out of the gritty TV series Sons of Anarchy.</p><p>A group of bikers wearing the patches and insignia of a motorcycle club surround an SUV in broad daylight near an intersection as the driver brings his vehicle to a halt.</p><p>One of the bikers gets off his Harley and confronts the motorist through the open driver’s side window. He alleges the man's vehicle had come into contact with his motorcycle — then beats him with fists and a helmet, and threatens him with a knife.</p><p>Several other bikers join the fray.</p><p>But this wasn’t a television moment. Court and police records show it was all too real, happening in June in normally sleepy Lake in the Hills, a far northwest suburb.</p><p>A 61-year-old Fox Lake man, who had been driving a Hyundai SUV, was bruised and battered but not hospitalized. He couldn’t be reached for comment but has described the experience as a “nightmare.”</p><p>At least some of the bikers were members or affiliates of the Calaveras Motorcycle Club. They left the scene but were later pulled over in Crystal Lake, and a single arrest was made — of Julio C. Salas, 36, of Sleepy Hollow, according to public records.</p><p>Salas, whose jacket identified him as a Calaveras “enforcer,” was charged with a number of crimes, including aggravated battery, unlawful restraint and mob action, the latter because Salas “knowingly and without legal justification participated in a mob action involving approximately 15-20 individuals riding motorcycles,” court records say.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-090000" name="image-090000"></a> <picture Salas, shown in his mug shot.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Lake in the Hills police</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Acting in concert with the group, the Defendant and other participants surrounded and encircled the victim’s vehicle, thereby forcing the victim to stop. The Defendant then knowingly and intentionally struck the victim in the face multiple times.”</p><p>Salas also “displayed a large knife during the altercation," which occurred near Virginia Road and Route 31, apparently after the bikers and the victim were turning at the intersection, then merging.</p><p>Salas told police that the driver had come into contact with his motorcycle, and an officer saw there was a “white horizontal scuff mark” on a saddlebag that may have indicated some contact.</p><p>A witness came up on the scene just as the confrontation was underway and said, if the SUV did clip the Harley, “I don’t think he did it intentionally,” but whatever occurred “it didn’t justify” the response by Salas.</p><p>“It was very upsetting,” the witness said, adding about the victim: “I was afraid for this man’s life.”</p><p>Salas’ lawyers asked the judge to restrict potential testimony that the bikers “belonged to a gang-related organization,” records show.</p><p>But before the trial could happen, Salas pleaded guilty to a single felony, aggravated battery, and the rest of the charges were dropped.</p><p>McHenry County prosecutors had wanted a minimum of two years in prison, but the judge gave him 180 days in jail. With time already served, he was released from custody. He was also given probation and a fine and ordered to undergo an anger management evaluation, records show.</p><p>At the sentencing hearing, held this month, Salas wept and apologized to the victim and, according to the Shaw Local publication, said: “I take full responsibility. entries.title: Reviving a 19th-century lumber hub through art in Clinton, Iowa
entries.summary: <p><i>Regenerative tourism harnesses the power of sustainable travel to transform places and communities for the better. In this series, we look at Midwestern towns and small cities that have leaned into tourism to help lift local economies and create destinations that travelers want to visit.</i></p><p>On the Mississippi River, just over 140 miles west of Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://www.growclinton.com/visiting/" target="_blank" ><u>Clinton</u></a> has seen many cycles of boom and bust since its settlement after the Louisiana Purchase. In the 19th century, railroads and ferries were drawn to Clinton, located where the river narrows. Then timber companies bought up vast swathes of Wisconsin and Minnesota and floated logs down the river to Clinton sawmills. Wealthy from lumber, the town claimed the most millionaires per capita in the country in the late 1800s before the upper Midwest was logged out.</p><p>Agribusiness eventually supplanted them, but in recent years there were significant vacancies and empty lots in the historic downtown, which has 17 buildings listed on the National Historic Register of Places including the Van Allen Building by Louis Sullivan.</p><p>“We are an industrial river town. We don’t hide from it. It has its war scars,” said Matt Parbs, the vice president of economic and community development for Grow Clinton, a nonprofit devoted to improving the local quality of life. “We’re finding a way to leverage our stories and our assets in the last five to 10 years.”</p><h3>The power of outdoor art</h3><p>Recently, that lever has been art. Through initiatives both grass roots and public, Clinton has seized on the power of outdoor exhibitions to not just attract out of towners but to instill pride in the locals.</p><p>Those investments were capped with the spring unveiling of three oversized trolls made of wood and organic refuse by the Dutch artist <a class="Link" href="https://www.thomasdambo.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Thomas Dambo</u></a>. (Chicagoans may be familiar with Dambo’s endearing trolls from an exhibition of them at the Morton Arboretum that closed in 2020). As Dambo tells it, the three trolls — Warren, Helmut and Marvin — woke up one morning to find the forest gone. They knew the trees had been taken to Clinton and decided to steal them back. Dispersed around the city, the roughly 20-foot-tall trolls are engaged in tree hugging and thievery.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure But lately, he's spent a lot of time on screen, with credits that include a role in Jordan Peele’s Academy Award-winning film "Get Out," NBC's "The Carmichael Show" and even his own sitcom, "Rel" on FOX.</p><p>Now, he's coming home. Last weekend, Howery filmed his latest standup special at Black Ensemble Theatre. The homecoming show is part of the What's Funny Comedy Festival, running through Saturday, which Howery cofounded with his former manager, Knowledge Beckom.</p><p>"Everything I’m doing the next few weeks in Chicago — the comedy festival, and I’m shooting a limited series that I wrote and created — it's a love letter to my family. It's my love letter to Chicago and to the way I grew up," Howery said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjtzz-l-dy/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's something every Cubs and Sox fan can agree on?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: Shelter-in-place ordered in Oswego after shots fired inside home during welfare check
entries.summary: <p>A shelter-in-place was ordered in Oswego after shots were fired inside a home during a welfare check early Friday. </p><p>A police presence was heavy where the incident happened in the 500 block of Colchester Drive and a shelter-in-place was ordered within a quarter mile around the area, according to the Oswego police department. </p><p>Officers responded to the area for a welfare check when a firearm was discharged inside a home, officials said. The individual is believed to be the only one inside the residence and no injuries were reported. </p><p><i>This is a developing story, check back for details. </i> </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Police release photo of purported sexual abuser on CTA bus in Little Italy
entries.summary: <p>Police have circulated a picture of a person they say 'inappropriately touched' a CTA bus passenger earlier this month in the Little Italy neighborhood.</p><p>The criminal sexual abuse happened aboard a CTA bus to a 48-year-old woman on Sept. 3 at 5:25 p.m. in the 1100 block of West Roosevelt Road. </p><p>Anyone with information, should reach Public Transportation Detectives at <a class="Link" href="tel:(312)%20745-4447" target="_blank" >(312)745-4447</a> or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com and use reference RD # JK399008. <br></p>

entries.title: Protesters rally against Trump's upcoming visit to Chicago area for golf tournament
entries.summary: <p>Roughly 100 protesters gathered near the Medinah Country Club in DuPage County Thursday morning, where President Donald Trump is expected to appear this Sunday during the final round of the Presidents Cup golf tournament — just over a year after Operation Midway Blitz first launched in the Chicago area.</p><p>One protester stood at the corner of Irving Park and Medinah Roads wearing only an Eagle mascot head and Speedos and holding a picket sign that read, "Stop Trump before he strips everything away."</p><p>"The Eagle is an American icon, right? So it's basically a stripped-down version of the eagle," the protester, a 44-year-old man who declined to share his name but goes by "Speedo Eagle Man," said. "It's basically the idea of Trump and his administration ... stripping things away from the American people."</p><p>The rally began sometime after 9:30 a.m. Protesters gathered for a variety of reasons, from decrying the administration's immigration enforcement tactics to voicing displeasure over inflation.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> entries.title: Chicago cop with UFC aspirations faces firing for sexually assaulting teenage girlfriend
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago cop and mixed martial arts fighter is facing dismissal from the police department after investigators found he sexually assaulted a teenager multiple times, new records show.</p><p>Officer Alberto Rodriguez met the woman around July 2018 when he was invited to her 18th birthday party by her brother, whom Rodriguez knew from an MMA gym, according to a report released this week by the Civilian Office of Police Accountability.</p><p>The two began talking and were in a relationship by the following spring, the woman told COPA.</p><p>It soon turned abusive and ended when police had to rescue the woman from Rodriguez’s home in August 2019 after she was held against her will, COPA said. She was 19 at the time.</p><p>COPA called for Rodriguez’s firing, finding his actions “egregious.” The oversight also found his version of events wasn’t credible.</p><p>“Officer Rodriguez’s actions caused physical and emotional harm … and are a discredit to the Department,” COPA wrote. “Furthermore, he took no accountability for any of his actions. Sexual assault and physical abuse cannot and should not be tolerated by the Department.”</p><p>A criminal investigation was initiated, according to a letter from former police Supt. Larry Snelling, but it doesn’t appear Rodriguez was ever charged with a crime.</p><p>He couldn’t be reached for comment.</p><p>On Aug. 5, 2019, the night before the woman was set to leave for a weekslong trip to Mexico, the pair went to dinner and returned to Rodriguez’s apartment, COPA said. When she told him she wanted to leave, he allegedly pushed her against a wall, took her keys, raped her and told her she’d “get used to it.”</p><p>Then on Aug. 23, 2019, after she returned from her trip, the two went to dinner again and Rodriguez bought her cocktails, knowing she was underage, COPA said.</p><p>Rodriguez then drove them to his home and raped her, according to COPA. She called her mother to pick her up in Wicker Park, but Rodriguez allegedly wouldn’t let her leave his apartment.</p><p>When the police showed up, Rodriguez refused to open the door, COPA said. Officers eventually got a key from Rodriguez’s father, who lived in the unit downstairs. Rodriguez was handcuffed and questioned, but not arrested, according to COPA.</p><p>Rodriguez had little professional fighting experience, going 3-1 by February 2022. But in an interview posted to the website of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, the country’s premier mixed martial arts organization, he said he planned to stay on the police force if he got called up to the UFC.</p><p>“I know that it’s obviously a very tough job, very stressful and that’s always going to be there and it’s only getting tougher with the times that are passing by, but I think that if I was ever to get into the UFC I would keep my job and keep being a good police officer and give as much back as I could,” Rodriguez said.</p><p>He now faces firing after Snelling agreed with COPA’s findings related to the alleged assaults.</p><p>Rodriguez is currently assigned to the department's alternate response section and remains stripped of his police powers.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/09/24/supreme-court-chicago-police-fraternal" target="_blank" >Illinois Supreme Court hears arguments in fight over Chicago police disciplinary process</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/21/chicago-police-cpd-vecchio-snelling" target="_blank" >Chicago cop with most misconduct complaints now charged with attacking woman as he faces firing</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/06/03/david-ross-larry-snelling-chicago-police-cpd-copa" target="_blank" >Chicago cop faces firing after passing test to join horseback unit while sidelined with ‘unbearable’ injury</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Hombre recibe libertad condicional por arrojar líquido a adolescentes de un estudio de baile folclórico en Avondale
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre se declaró culpable de cargos de agresión menor por arrojar un balde con líquido sobre adolescentes y padres en un estudio de danza folclórica del noroeste de la ciudad, según registros judiciales.</p><p>Robert Villanueva, de 50 años, fue sentenciado a seis meses de libertad condicional después de declararse culpable el miércoles de cinco cargos de agresión menor, según registros de la Corte del condado de Cook. Originalmente había sido <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/03/12/acusan-a-hombre-de-lanzar-liquido-a-estudiantes-de-un-estudio-de-baile-folclorico-en-chicago" target="_blank" >acusado en marzo</a> por el incidente.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/DVlni0ujtsT/" target="_blank" >Un video del incidente publicado en redes sociales</a> muestra a Villanueva y a una mujer, que no fue acusada, en una escalera trasera mientras gritaban: “Tienen suerte de que ICE no está aquí”. Luego Villanueva arroja vasos con líquido hacia el grupo, que salía de Ballet Folklórico, un estudio de danza folclórica mexicana en Avondale.</p><p>A principios de este año, la Policía de Chicago dijo que las víctimas eran un niño de 13 años, tres niñas de 13, 14 y 15 años, y tres mujeres de 43, 41 y 40 años. En ese momento, la policía indicó que había otras víctimas en el lugar que no aparecían en el informe.</p><p>La libertad condicional de Villanueva terminará en marzo, apenas unas semanas después del aniversario del incidente.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Cubs-Red Sox game Sunday might move to Tropicana Field, which is preparing to host
entries.summary: <p>The Cubs' wild weekend is underway, and it could get wilder. </p><p>With a Nor'easter threatening Boston, where the Cubs were scheduled to finish the regular season this weekend, the Rays' Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida, is standing by to host the game Sunday. </p><p>FOX 13 Tampa Bay reported Friday that the Trop's operations teams are preparing to handle "security, concessions, ticketing and neutral-site venue branding," among other logistical needs, to host Game 162. </p><p>The Cubs and Red Sox are scheduled to play a split doubleheader Friday. After the nightcap, the Cubs are set to fly to St. Pete. The day game Friday was moved from Sunday, with the game Saturday night still scheduled. </p><p>Now that game appears close to being moved to Sunday, giving the teams a day off Saturday after playing three games in two days. The Red Sox will have played three games in 24 hours after playing a night game Thursday. </p><p>MLB is doing everything it can to get the series in because of its impact on seeding in the National League wild-card picture. The Padres hold the top spot and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. They're one game ahead of the Cubs and two ahead of the Phillies. The Cubs own the tiebreaker over both. </p><p>The Diamondbacks are trying to crash the party. They're the only NL team outside the playoff picture still alive, and they're visiting the Padres this weekend. </p><p>The wild-card round is scheduled to run Tuesday to Thursday, after a day off Monday.</p>

entries.title: Man dies, two women injured in Englewood blaze
entries.summary: <p>The cause of a fire at an Englewood home that left a 55-year-old man dead and two women, 81 and 19, injured Friday morning is under investigation. </p><p>Police and firefighters were called to the 500 block of West 66th Street about 7:30 a.m. and began to help rescue people and battle the fire. </p><p>Three occupants of the home included a 55-year-old man who was taken to St.Bernard Hospital where he was pronounced dead and two woman, 81 and 19, who were listed in fair condition at Holy Cross Hospital, police said. </p><p>No one else was hurt and there were no reports of displacements, according to police. </p><p>The cause of the fire remained under investigation. </p>

entries.title: 2 beluga whales had 'chronic gastrointestinal disease' before death, Shedd reveals
entries.summary: <p>Two of the four Shedd Aquarium beluga whales that have died in recent weeks suffered from a “chronic gastrointestinal disease” — a sickness that likely developed before they arrived here from a Canadian aquatic park, Shedd staff announced Friday.</p><p>A third beluga, 34-year-old Beethoven, suffered from age-related health problems, Shedd said. Beethoven, unlike the other two, was part of the aquarium’s resident population.</p><p>Shedd also said veterinarians have found no evidence of a “shared infectious disease or common environmental factor connecting” the deaths of Beethoven, Peekachu and Rain.</p><p>“These initial findings do not always lead to one definitive cause of death. However, the evidence can still provide meaningful insight into an animal’s health, identify conditions that may have contributed to a loss and inform the care of other animals,” Shedd said in a statement. “We want to share what the evidence can and cannot establish, and how we are applying what we learn to the care of the belugas at Shedd.”</p><p>Shedd took in a total of 10 belugas from Marineland, adding to the eight resident whales. </p><p>"No animal is where we want them to be clinically, but we are fortified by the incremental, step-by-step progress, which is often not linear," the aquarium said in its statement. "Secord and Caspian remain the whales of greatest clinical concern at this time, and our teams continue to monitor them and the other rescued belugas around the clock."</p><p>Peekachu, a 23-year-old female, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/26/one-of-the-shedds-rescued-beluga-whales-has-died" >died Aug. 25</a>, and Rain, a 20-year-old female, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/09/03/shedd-aquarium-beluga" >died Sept. 2</a>. A total of four belugas, including three at Shedd, have died since being transported out of the shuttered Marineland Canada during the summer. One of those, Osiris, a 26-year-old female, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/09/21/3rd-beluga-whale-dies-shedd-aquarium-moved-marineland-canada-niagara-falls" >died Monday at Shedd</a>. Jelly Bean, another rescued beluga, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/09/18/3rd-beluga-dies-marineland-canada-shedd-aquarium" >died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain</a> earlier this month.</p><p>Animal rights activists in the United States and Canada have questioned whether the belugas were healthy enough to endure the stress of being transferred out of Marineland — in trucks and then airplanes. Shedd’s preliminary medical findings will likely only raise further questions about the rescue and the health of the belugas before they left Canada.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/22/belugas-chicago-shedd-aquarium-marineland-canada-rescue" >Rescued belugas have arrived in Chicago. The move is unprecedented — and controversial</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Shedd is part of a consortium of four U.S. and one Spanish aquarium that together agreed to take 30 belugas languishing in Marineland, located in Niagara Falls, Canada. Marineland had faced criticism for years that its animals were living in unsanitary conditions.</p><p>The park closed to the public in 2024, and Marineland officials, citing extreme financial difficulties, had threatened to euthanize the whales if permanent homes couldn’t be found.</p>

entries.title: ‘Broadview Six’ prosecutor slams Boutros in resignation letter, saying he pushed doomed felony charges
entries.summary: <p>Ending her nearly two-decade career<b> </b>as a federal prosecutor this week, Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg made clear to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/07/chicago-crime-justice-department-doj-boutros-trump-midway-blitz-corruption" target="_blank" >U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros</a> that “this is not a voluntary departure.”</p><p>Rather, the prosecutor at the center of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six”</a> scandal wrote in a three-page letter<b> </b>that she was retiring “under protest.”<b> </b>She complained that she’d become “a convenient target to be scapegoated and publicly vilified.”<b> </b></p><p>And ultimately, she said, she decided to defend herself.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/24/broadview-six-sheri-mecklenburg" >‘Broadview Six’ prosecutor ‘owns’ mistakes in tainted case, says she was following orders</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“You have forced me to choose between remaining silent while my professional reputation is destroyed and prematurely surrendering my cherished career,” Mecklenburg told Boturos.<b> </b>“I choose the latter.”</p><p>Along the way, Mecklenburg alleged that Boutros had laid “responsibility at my feet for a felony prosecution that you personally directed over my objection that the case was better suited to misdemeanor charges.” </p><p>That prompted a swift denial Friday from the Justice Department.</p><p>"The claim that AUSA Mecklenburg proposed a misdemeanor and was told instead to file a felony charge is false," it said in a statement. "Mecklenburg's recommendation in writing to the supervisory chain of the U.S. Attorney's Office included the [conspiracy] felony as the strongest charge."</p><p>Defense attorneys for the former “Broadview Six” defendants will still surely seize upon the claim, one of many still to be litigated as the case heats up again in the courtroom of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" target="_blank" >U.S. District Judge April Perry</a>. The judge has said <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/23/broadview-six-boutros-perry" target="_blank" >she’ll hear arguments Thursday</a><b> </b>over the potential consequences of the tainted prosecution of six Operation Midway Blitz protesters.</p><p>Questions about who directed the prosecution have swirled ever since the indictment was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >made public Oct. 29</a>, in the midst of the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign in the Chicago area.</p><p>Six people from a larger crowd were accused of conspiring to impede a federal agent<b> </b>on Sept. 26, 2025. Many of the six were involved in local Democratic politics, raising questions about selective prosecution.</p><p>Boutros has acknowledged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/05/boutros-broadview-six-perry" target="_blank" >“mistakes were made”</a><b> </b>in the case, but he said he’s implemented reforms to prevent them from happening again and launched an inquiry into Mecklenburg’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/22/broadview-six-damage-spreads-boutros-drops-more-charges-details-ongoing-review" target="_blank" >nearly 20 years of work</a>.</p><div Dick Durbin/YouTube</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Mecklenburg <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/24/broadview-six-sheri-mecklenburg" target="_blank" >broke her silence</a> through a court filing Thursday, after Perry announced plans for the hearing. Mecklenburg’s attorneys<b> </b>said<b> </b>she<b> </b>“owns”<b> </b>her mistakes<b> </b>but complained of attempts by the former defendants in the case<b> </b>to<b> </b>“smear her with meritless accusations.”</p><p>The ex-prosecutor is seeking to participate in the litigation<b> </b>if Perry grants<b> </b>certain defense motions, including for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/17/broadview-6-want-special-counsel-to-probe-boutros-office-trumps-justice-department-for-criminal-contempt" target="_blank" >special counsel</a> who would investigate Boutros, Mecklenburg and others.</p><p>Mecklenburg’s attorneys disclosed that Boutros’ office threatened her with discipline<b> </b>or firing<b> </b>if she intervened in the case. Instead, she announced her immediate retirement. Now, the Chicago Sun-Times has obtained a copy of her letter to Boutros.</p><p>The document, dated Thursday, is Mecklenburg’s most substantive response to the public condemnation she’s experienced since misconduct allegations against her rocked the Dirksen Federal Courthouse.</p><p>Mecklenburg is accused of speaking to grand jurors outside of the grand jury room, as well as engaging in a forbidden practice called “vouching” while seeking an indictment against the “Broadview Six.”<b> </b>Her attorneys acknowledged those “mistakes”<b> </b>in their filing<b> </b>Thursday.</p><p>Vouching occurs when prosecutors put their personal credibility on the line to support criminal charges. Grand jurors are expected to hand up indictments based on evidence, not the goodwill of a prosecutor who already has the upper hand in the grand jury room.</p><p>The former prosecutor is also accused of excusing grand jurors who didn’t agree with the government’s case — an allegation Mecklenburg denies.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/01/broadview-six-midway-blitz-abughazaleh-straw-rabbit-perry-trump-ice-crime" target="_blank" >Charged in the case were</a> then-congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, then-Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, musician<b> </b>Joselyn Walsh and<b> </b>Abughazaleh campaign worker Andre<b> </b>Martin.</p><p>All charges against them have been dropped.</p><p>Mecklenburg told Boutros “it would be false and profoundly misleading”<b> </b>to suggest she was leaving the U.S. attorney’s office over “false accusations”<b> </b>or an investigation of her conduct.</p><p>Rather, she pointed to “the incredible damage”<b> </b>Boutros’ statements about the case have done to her career. She told him that, “preventing me from defending myself is particularly reprehensible given the office’s failure to adequately defend me.”</p><p>“I repeatedly sought guidance from, kept informed, and followed the directions of the front office — including you — at every consequential stage,” Mecklenburg wrote.</p><p>Mecklenburg<b> </b>withdrew from the case<b> </b>in February. Perry discovered the alleged misconduct by reading transcripts of the grand jury proceedings<b> </b>in late May. Boutros’ office had previously given the judge redacted copies of the transcripts, after Mecklenburg’s departure.</p><p>That prompted claims of a cover-up by Boutros’ office. Mecklenburg noted in her letter that, “no one consulted me about any transcript redactions.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure media.</p><p>“I would have expected the leadership of the office to ensure that a career prosecutor whose conduct and reputation were about to be publicly condemned received notice and an opportunity to be heard,” Mecklenburg wrote. “Had I been afforded that basic fairness at the outset, I believe matters would not have reached this point.”</p><p>Rather, Mecklenburg told Boutros, “you recklessly agreed in court that I had committed misconduct without even asking for my account, fully reviewing the record or briefing the law.”</p><p>She complained that he “sent an office-wide email laying responsibility at my feet for a felony prosecution that you personally directed over my objection that the case was better suited to misdemeanor charges. You then publicly announced an investigation of my conduct spanning twenty years.</p><p>“These inexplicable actions severely damaged a reputation I worked hard to build over decades and have damaged my prospects for future employment and income,” Mecklenburg wrote.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/23/broadview-six-boutros-mecklenburg-loretto-hospital" >As ‘Broadview Six’ prosecutor faces reckoning, Boutros yet to escape cloud hanging over his office</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The retiring prosecutor wrote that she’d “never received written notice explaining the basis for placing me — and only me — on leave.</p><p>“I was given no meaningful opportunity to respond,”<b> </b>she wrote, “before being publicly condemned by you.”</p><p>Finally, Mecklenburg said she’s “prepared to address legitimate scrutiny of my actions.</p><p>“But legitimate scrutiny is not the same as scapegoating, and accountability does not require silence in the face of demonstrably false accusations,” she wrote.<b> </b>“I still expect a full and fair opportunity to address the allegations against me and restore my reputation.”</p><p>She noted that she “would have expected, at some point during the past four months, that the leaders who directed or approved the prosecution would accept responsibility for their own roles and decisions rather than assigning the consequences to me alone.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/b2/7f/030ba5b34759b1727d86282f51f7/shmfull.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: Painting along Red Line was a Lake View homecoming for artist Anthony Lewellen
entries.summary: <p>CTA Red Line riders through <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lakeview" >Lake View</a> have a new mural to catch just east of the Sheridan stop.</p><p>Artist Anthony Lewellen — also known by his graffiti name Antck — added a bright and welcoming pop of color stretching 80 feet across and 26 feet up the wall behind the Nourishing Hope building at 3945 N. Sheridan Road. Neighbors grasp hands, hand off groceries and gather around a circular table. Big bright circles within circles of various colors, Lewellen’s signature shape, billow behind the scenes.</p><p>The Red Line rumbles directly across the way from the three-story painting, all done View.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Mitzi Baum, CEO of Nourishing Hope, says, “He really captured what we do."</p><p>Nourishing Hope opened in 1970 as The People’s Pantry of Lake View. Now, it’s one of Chicago’s largest relief organizations and provides food, mental health and social services to those who need it. It employs more than 60 people and has 7,000 volunteers. The organization opened Sheridan Market, which offers fresh food and social services, in its Sheridan Road home in 2016.</p><p>The mural came about, Baum says, after she started wandering neighborhoods during the pandemic, photographing murals and posting them to her Instagram account. As she grew to appreciate and support Chicago’s public art, she realized the wall of Nourishing Hope’s Sheridan Market home was primed for adding one of their own.</p><p>For Lewellen it was a homecoming of sorts, as he grew up near the corner of West Addison and North Fremont streets and remembers when the building housed a hip-hop shoe store. The back wall was painted by a New York artist at the time, he says.</p><p>Last summer, as he painted the Nourishing Hope mural, titled “Radiating Hope,” the sounds of the trains rumbling by reminded him of being a kid. “It’s a comforting sound for me," he says.</p><p>He says his biggest challenge was making the Nourishing Hope logo look like it was centered within a radial with the “O” in “Hope.” However, the O in Hope is not centered, so the trick was to position the word and the radial to disguise that fact.</p><p>Lewellen says he hopes the mural is a “source of inspiration and joy and a nice pop of color for the neighborhood for years to come.”</p><p>Alderman Angela Clay, who represents the 46th Ward, says the mural illustrated what Nourishing Hope is known for.</p><p>“You never know who’s going to walk through the door, but you know you’re going to serve them,” she says.</p><p>Baum says, “I hope it brings joy to you every time you see it.”</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Bears still proceeding with Case Keenum as starting QB vs. Eagles as Caleb Williams, Tyson Bagent remain out
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> backup quarterback Tyson Bagent was back in the building Friday, but not at practice. With Bagent still in the concussion protocol, third-stringer Case Keenum remained in line to start Monday against the Eagles as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/11/as-engineer-and-artist-blend-styles-bears-ben-johnson-gets-goosebumps-about-future-with-caleb-williams" >Caleb Williams</a> recovers from a hamstring strain.</p><p>While Williams likely will be out and still could miss multiple games, the Bears are hopeful Bagent could be cleared and are preparing him as much as possible behind the scenes.</p><p>Offensive coordinator Press Taylor said the extra day between games increases the chances “to get him back healthy” and for all the quarterbacks to “dive into the game plan a little bit more.”</p><p>The Bears also have explored which non-quarterbacks could play if needed. The NFL reinstituted the emergency third quarterback rule in 2023, but coach Ben Johnson said the team won’t add anyone and would proceed with Keenum as the starter and practice-squad quarterback Miller Moss behind him if necessary.</p><p>“In the spring, when we have all those skill guys throw, we put stock into that,” Taylor said. “We have an idea who has a past of throwing, who's played baseball, who played high school quarterback, and then we watch them throw.”</p><p>Tight end Cole Kmet was a contingency early in his career and threw a pass last season. Wide receiver Rome Odunze played quarterback until high school, and running back Roschon Johnson was a high school quarterback.</p><p>Keenum, 38, hasn’t played since 2023 and rarely, if ever, would’ve gotten snaps against the first-team defense in practices.</p><p>“He’s still got pop in his arm and is able to drive throws down the field, so you see it in the routes on air or the one-on-ones,” quarterbacks coach J.T. Barrett said. “He’s still got a lot in the tank as far as throwing the ball downfield.”</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Chicago police search Glenwood business tied to owners of South Chicago Chapel
entries.summary: <p>A south suburban cremation business owned by a couple under investigation for mishandling human remains was searched as part of a "follow-up" investigation by Chicago police on Thursday.</p><p>Planet Green Cremations in Glenwood is a storefront that contracted cremation services for families and is owned by Clark and Johanna Morgan. Chicago police officers and Area 2 detectives executed a search warrant at the business, 319 E. Glenwood Lansing Rd., Thursday as part of a “follow-up investigation.”</p><p>Chicago police did not say what was found inside the business but officers were seen carrying out several boxes.</p><p>The couple is under investigation after 56 bodies were discovered in various stages of decomposition last month at South Chicago Chapel on the city's Far South Side. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" >state shut down</a> the funeral home on Aug. 6 after receiving a tip that the Morgans were improperly storing bodies.</p><p>Planet Green Cremations was not actually a crematory, according to Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza’s office. Instead, the Morgans used the business to arrange for cremations through a third party. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/28/sisters-mothers-cremated-remains-south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home" target="_blank" >Families would then pick up their loved ones’</a> cremated remains at Planet Green.</p><p>Mendoza’s office said the “storefronts” are not regulated by the state but are required to have a licensed funeral director on staff or under contract to oversee the removal of bodies, prepare death certificates and organize transportation to a cemetery or crematory.</p><p>Planet Green often arranged for cremations to be done by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/09/bohemian-national-cemetery-under-investigation-for-improperly-stored-remains-equipment-failures" target="_blank" >Bohemian National Cemetery</a>, on Chicago's Northwest Side, another crematory under investigation for the improper storage of human remains.</p><p>Mendoza’s office said at least 22 out of 35 bodies discovered at Bohemian “involved the Morgans in some way” – 10 came from South Chicago Chapel and 12 from Planet Green.</p><p>Last year, Mendoza’s office shut down another of the Morgans’ businesses, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" target="_blank" >Heights Crematory</a> in south suburban Chicago Heights, after finding that the couple had mishandled human remains. </p><p>While Mendoza's office oversees crematories, the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation licenses funeral directors and embalmers. </p><p>After shutting down the Chicago Heights business, Mendoza’s office said it “urged” the IDFPR to revoke Johanna Morgan’s funeral director’s license. The office also said it turned its findings over to law enforcement “in hopes of criminal charges being filed against the Morgans.”</p><p>Also Thursday, a Cook County judge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/24/judge-orders-new-inspection-of-south-deering-funeral-home-where-56-bodies-found" target="_blank" >ordered another inspection</a> of South Chicago Chapel and barred the Morgans from using, renting or leasing the funeral home at 2939 E. 95th St.</p><p>Judge Federico Rodriguez made the orders during a hearing at the Richard J. Daley Center after the city sued the Morgans over alleged building code violations at the now-shuttered South Deering business.</p><p>City attorneys said the building has not been inspected since the initial inspection, which followed the discovery of the bodies. The city wants the new inspection to take place Oct. 23 and include an examination of the building’s interior.</p><p>Rodriguez ordered the Morgans to be present in person for the inspection.</p>
entries.author: Cindy Hernandez

entries.title: Bears report: K Cairo Santos sits out, RB Kyle Monangai full participant
entries.summary: <p>Here's what happened Friday at Halas Hall:</p><h3>Santos still out </h3><p>Kicker Cairo Santos, who made a surprise appearance on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ projected injury report Thursday, did not practice Friday, either. He has a right hip problem. Special teams coordinator Richard Hightower didn't elaborate, other than to say that he was "obviously dealing with something."</p><p>The Bears have yet to add a placekicker to their roster but would have to by 3 p.m. Monday if Santos isn’t in their plans. Jake Moody, who kicked in two games for an injured Santos last year, remains available.</p><h3>Monangai, Stevenson practice</h3><p>Running back Kyle Monangai (right knee) seems good to go for Monday. He was a full participant Friday. Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson (hamstring) practiced, albeit it on a limited basis, one day after the projected injury report said he would not have participated.</p><p>Linebacker Noah Sewell (Achilles' tendon) and defensive lineman Shemar Turner (knee) were both limited but can't return until Week 5.</p><h3>Rule change?</h3><p>Hightower and fellow NFL’s special teams coordinators met virtually late Friday to discuss a potential rule change. Last year, the league’s new kickoff rule allowed for a 12<sup>th</sup> player to hold the ball on the tee in case of weather. During the offseason, the league allowed it regardless of weather.</p><p>Last week, the Eagles had Braden Mann hold Jake Elliott’s ball at an angle — and not on a tee — to make for a nastier squib kick. The Falcons did it in Week 1. Hightower said that was against "the intent of the rule." It wouldn't be surprising if the rule was re-written with a more clear directive.</p>

entries.title: 2026 Cubs, White Sox join short list in Chicago baseball history — their postseason stays might be short, too
entries.summary: <p>Think about all the pieces that had to fall into place for the Cubs and White Sox to clinch playoff berths within two minutes of each other Thursday. That includes the Cubs overcoming all sorts of pitching challenges and the Sox overcoming years of ineptitude.</p><p>Yet there they were, celebrating simultaneously, the Cubs at home and the Sox in Kansas City. It was a surreal visual, marking only the fourth time in history that the teams made the playoffs in the same season.</p><p>Think about that, too. In more than 125 years of coexistence, the Cubs and Sox have played in the same postseason only three times.</p><p>“When I first heard that, it was pretty amazing,” Sox general manager Chris Getz said Friday.</p><p>Getz and Cubs baseball president Jed Hoyer are good friends, and they exchanged text messages during the historic day.</p><p>“I guess maybe he was a better friend; he texted me first,” Getz said. “I didn’t even know what was going on in their situation.”</p><p>Of the four times, this was the unlikeliest, considering the Sox lost more than 100 games in 2023-25. The last time was in 2020, the pandemic-shortened season, when the teams clinched five days apart. In 2008, they clinched 10 days apart, with the Sox needing two extra days because of a rainout and a one-game playoff for the division title.</p><p>The first time was in 1906, when the teams won their respective pennants 14 days apart. No silly wild-card round back then. Do not pass “Go,” and head straight to the World Series. Though the Cubs (116-36-3) won 23 more games than the Sox (93-58), the Sox won the series 4-2. The thing is, none of us saw it, so it’s hard to appreciate it.</p><p>But just imagine it.</p><p>“If they were to play each other in the World Series,” Steve Stone said, “it would be one of the great things to ever happen to the city of Chicago.”</p><p>Stone knows a thing or two about Chicago baseball. Outside of three years pitching for the Orioles (1979-81), he has been a Cubs or Sox player or a Cubs or Sox broadcaster almost every year since 1973.</p><p>“I’ve very much fallen in love with this city,” Stone said. “I love to see both sides of town celebrating.”</p><p>But one has more reason to celebrate.</p><p>“The Cubs were supposed to be there; the White Sox were not,” Stone said.</p><p>Indeed, but the Sox appear to have the easier path to success in the postseason.</p><p>The Sox have a better bullpen and less-intimidating competition, whether they end up winning the division or landing in the wild-card round. A division title gives them the No. 2 seed and a spot in the American League Division Series, where they could face the Astros, Guardians or Rangers, teams on their level.</p><p>The Cubs might have the best offense and defense in baseball, but bad pitching can sabotage both. Like Harry Caray used to say, “What about the pitching?” Then there’s the Cubs’ competition in the National League with superpowers such as the Braves, Brewers and Dodgers. But before facing any of them, the Cubs must survive the wild-card round.</p><p>Still, crazy things happen in the postseason. Teams get on a roll, and there’s no stopping them. Sox fans remember the 2005 team, which went 11-1 in the postseason and won the World Series. Cubs fans recall the 2016 team, which rallied in every round of the playoffs and won the World Series.</p><p>Imagine them meeting in the Series 120 years later.</p><p>“We’ve had some clubhouse staff born and raised in Chicago,” said Sox pitcher Davis Martin, the team’s longest-tenured player. “I always asked, what would a White Sox-Cubs World Series do? [They’d say,] I don’t know if the city of Chicago could handle it.”</p><p>“I think traffic would be out of control,” Getz said.</p><p>Probably, but what’s really out of control is the city’s fondness for teams that won little or nothing. The 2016 Cubs and 2005 Sox could use some company.</p><p>Cubs fans of a certain age grew up hearing how incredible the summer of 1969 was, only to learn that the team fell apart in September and lost the division to those dastardly Mets. The 1983 Sox might be even more celebrated than the 2005 champs, and they lost to the Orioles in the AL Championship Series.</p><p>But it’s unlikely that either team will get to the World Series. Still, it should be fun finding out — perhaps more for one team than the other.</p><p>“If both teams get knocked out in the first round,” Stone said, “it will be a major disappointment for the Cubs, and it will be something that Sox fans will appreciate having gotten there.”</p>

entries.summary: <p>Families staying at Ronald McDonald House at Lurie Children’s Hospital have a new game room thanks to Chicago Bulls guard Josh Giddey.</p><p>The Josh Giddey Family Foundation and the Chicago Bulls unveiled the transformed community space on Friday.</p><p>“It's a colorful game room with a lot of Chicago Bulls and Australia-themed activities,” said Giddey, who is from Australia, entries.title: Construction sign displaying anti-Riot Fest messages appears near Douglass Park, echoing local frustrations
entries.summary: <p>A traffic sign stationed near Douglass Park is displaying anti-Riot Fest messages on the day the park was originally supposed to be cleaned and reopened to the public.</p><p>The digital sign sat in the grassy area in the 2900 block of South Marshall Boulevard, just north of West Cermak Road and a few blocks south of where the entrance to the park was cordoned off by gates as cleanup extended to Tuesday. </p><p>The latch to the computer that controlled the sign sat undone while the messages saying, "Pro riot, anti fest," "Gentrify GTFO Douglass" and "Go home Yankee" were visible. </p><p>The sign is the latest manifestation of residents' frustrations with the prolonged cleanup and aftermath of the annual festival, which has called the park home for nearly a decade and is contracted through 2027.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-860000" Road, and just blocks south of where the park still was gated off as cleanup continued after the festival Friday, September 25, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Violet Miller/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Chicago Department of Transportation explained the sign wasn't city-owned. Riot Fest declined a request for comment.</p><p>On the <a class="Link" href="https://riotfest.org/park-impact/#access" target="_blank" ><u>Riot Fest website,</u></a> the original 2026 timeline had set Sept. 21-24 for production load-out, cleaning and restoration, with Sept. 25 listed as a date the park would reopen to the public. But completing the load-out has since been pushed to Sept. 29, “weather and ground conditions permitting,” according to the festival site.</p><p>On Friday, vehicles were traveling through open portions of the park, where the grounds were still muddy and mangled a week after the fest began. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/21/riot-fest-cleanup-douglass-park-mud" >Cleanup begins in Douglass Park after rain-soaked Riot Fest left it a mud pit</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-and-culture/2025/04/09/riot-fest-three-year-deal-chicago-park-district-douglass-park" >Riot Fest 3-year deal to remain in Douglass Park approved by Chicago Park District</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The Chicago Park District Board of Commissioners <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-and-culture/2025/04/09/riot-fest-three-year-deal-chicago-park-district-douglass-park" target="_blank" >approved a new three-year deal</a> in April 2025 after the festival briefly planned a move to a sports stadium in the suburbs before ultimately coming back to Douglass Park. It had been held in Humboldt Park for years, but was forced to change locations after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/5/4/18556684/riot-fest-claims-damage-to-humboldt-park-repaired-preventive-measures-in-place" >complaints of similar damage</a> following the 2014 iteration of the festival.</p><p>Park district officials said it will generate roughly $3 million to $4.5 million over the course of the three-year deal via annual permit fees, as the festival has to provide a cut of ticket sales to the city.</p><p>From the money raised, the park district has a 30% “give back” policy in place for Douglass Park, meaning $900,000 to $1.2 million is allocated solely for improvements to the North Lawndale grounds. The contract also stipulates Riot Fest will give an additional 10% toward “capital improvements in Douglass Park.”</p><p>But residents <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2024/09/19/neighbors-riot-fest-douglass-park-traffic-crowds-music" target="_blank" >who live near Douglass Park have long complained </a>of traffic congestion, trash, noise, and interruptions to the area that is also in proximity to two hospitals. Earlier this week, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/21/riot-fest-cleanup-douglass-park-mud" >residents told the Sun-Times</a> the events disrupt after-school activities and local youth sports leagues while not actually investing in the community.</p><p>Among them is Susan Mullen, who has lived near Douglass Park since 1989. </p><p>She said "public spaces should be public spaces, never privatized for profit" and that the streets needed to be clear for the hospitals "where seconds make a difference."</p><p>"I like music. I'm not against Riot Fest. May they live long and prosper somewhere else," said Mullen, who was kept from seeing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/20/riot-fest-day-3-douglass-park" >William Shatner’s metal band</a> at the festival last weekend because of rain and mud. "But the hospitals aren't gonna move, so what does? It has to be Riot Fest."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-790000" entries.title: Reading the tea leaves on Sky coach Tyler Marsh’s future
entries.summary: <p>The Sparks’ Lynne Roberts was the first coach to get the ax after the WNBA’s regular season ended. She was fired Friday.</p><p>Given that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> recent disappointments have resembled the Sparks’, one has to wonder: Will coach Tyler Marsh suffer the same fate?</p><p>The Sky lost their final game Thursday, finishing the season 16-28. During Marsh’s postgame news conference, amid the usual flood of emotions brought about by the end of a season, there was also an added sense that his future hung in the balance.</p><p>It can’t be a comfortable moment for Marsh, 38.</p><p>He told the Sun-Times recently that, for a longtime NBA assistant who found a greater purpose in the WNBA, leading this team is his dream come true.</p><p>The question is whether that feeling is reciprocated from the top.</p><p>Marsh’s exit meeting with the higher-ups is scheduled for Saturday morning.</p><p>When asked Thursday why he’s the right person to lead the organization into its next chapter, he was characteristically deferential.</p><p>‘‘We’ve been able to see some level of improvement from Year 1 to Year 2, but it’s less about me stating my case and just letting you know that I love this team,’’ he said. ‘‘I love being the head coach of this team. I don’t take it for granted or lightly.</p><p>‘‘I’ve hoped to have had some impact on our players and our community and our fan base and our front office and our support staff, and I’ll let the chips fall where [they] may.</p><p>‘‘I’m not the decision-maker. If I’m back, I will continue to give it my all. And if I’m not, then that’s the decision that is made, and I will be grateful for the two years that I’ve had.’’</p><p>Surely, Marsh has noticed the warning signs coming from above. General manager Jeff Pagliocca has held fast to his belief that injuries shouldn’t have prevented a playoff appearance, which implicates Marsh.</p><p>The Sky’s history of churn also looms over him. If Marsh is let go, it would represent the Sky’s eighth coaching change since their founding in 2005, tied with the Sparks for the most during that period.</p><p>Will support from his players help buck that trend?</p><p>During their exit interviews Friday, players reiterated their usual praise. Marsh helped to facilitate a positive locker-room environment and cares deeply about the team. He has a talent for drawing up plays out of timeouts and putting people in positions to succeed.</p><p>Those are real compliments, but none of his stars was exactly pounding the table in his favor, either. The strongest defense came from veteran Natasha Cloud, who pointed out that Marsh deserves grace as a second-year coach and inherited a ‘‘s--- show’’ when he arrived in Chicago.</p><p>Then she stated the obvious: This decision is way above her pay grade.</p><p>It’s clearly one the organization needs to get right. They’ve got a nice young core in Rickea Jackson, Kamilla Cardoso and Sydney Taylor and roster continuity to capitalize on next season. But Cloud’s ‘‘s--- show’’ comment should remind everyone that the roots of the Sky’s dysfunction extend beyond Marsh and that real change will require a collective effort.</p><p>Marsh alluded to that when he was asked Thursday about the biggest step forward the organization took this season.</p><p>‘‘I think that in order for us to move forward as an organization, there has to be a realization of what has held us back,’’ he said. ‘‘There has to be our own self-reflection and evaluation organizationally, so that we can understand how to attract and address things moving forward.</p><p>‘‘So I think that being able to have those hard conversations behind the scenes will serve as the turning point going forward.’’</p><p>Marsh might not be willing to make a fuss about why he deserves to return for a third season, but good for him for not letting the higher-ups off the hook, either.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Whomever plays QB for the Bears has to deal with Vic Fangio
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> offensive coordinator Press Taylor is perhaps the premier archivist of plays in the NFL. And no opposing play-caller takes up more room in his files than Vic Fangio, the longest tenured defensive mind in the league.</p><p>Fangio, who suffocated the Chiefs to win his first Super Bowl two years ago with the Eagles, is in his 26<sup>th</sup> year as the defensive play-caller across eight teams. His 2018 Bears defense was one of the best in franchise history and landed him the Broncos head coaching job.</p><p>He’s spawned acolytes that now call plays for the Panthers, whom the Bears played in Week 1, and the Saints, among others. No one does it quite like the original, though, as whomever plays quarterback for the Bears on Monday night will likely find out.</p><p>Case Keenum was the only <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/25/bears-still-proceeding-with-case-keenum-as-starting-qb-vs-eagles-as-caleb-williams-tyson-bagent-remain-out" target="_blank" >quarterback on the Bears’ active roster</a> to practice Friday. Tyson Bagent, who is in concussion protocol, reported to Halas Hall but didn’t step foot on the practice field. Caleb Williams, who is not practicing this week after pulling his hamstring Sunday, is unlikely to face the Eagles.</p><p>The Bears face a distinctively different challenge than last week, when Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores blitzed Williams 77% of the time. Fangio has blitzed only 18% of the time this year.</p><p>“Different style,” running back D’Andre Swift said. “If they want to do some things that the Vikings did, bring it on.”</p><p>Fangio won’t. His defense usually features a two-high safety shell that allows the Eagles to rotate their defensive backs to confuse the quarterback,</p><p>“They play tricks on your eyes,” Keenum said. “They do a really good job pre- and post-snap, and there’s not a lot of tells to tell you what the coverage is going to be beforehand.”</p><p>They key is patience, Taylor said.</p><p>“You're not going to get these big, long explosives the way they play in the shell …” he said. “They just do a great job of playing a variety of different fronts and techniques ultimately to try to do the same idea at the end of the day — limit the explosives and make you go the long, hard way.</p><p>“It's hard to go 14, 15 plays and score on a drive. And so that's kind of what they force you to do the way they play. And then they've got really, really good players, too.”</p><p>Jalen Carter might be the best. After the defensive lineman fell from his projection as the No. 1 pick in 2023, the Bears had a chance to draft him ninth — and traded back one spot to the Eagles. The Bears’ pick, Darnell Wright, has turned into one of the NFL’s best right tackles. However, the Bears are still searching for an impact defensive lineman four seasons later.</p><p>The Eagles have two. Nose tackle Jordan Davis got a three-year, $78 million extension in March, tying him for second-most among all interior linemen.</p><p>“Up front, those are some of the best two guys up front that are playing the game right now,” Keenum said. “And I think all over the board, you look at playmakers that they have on the defense, so we’ve got our work cut out for us.</p><p>Carter, who has a cast on his wrist, “did better than I thought he would” while playin against the Titans, Fangio said. Their most dangerous edge rusher, Jonathan Greenard, still hasn’t played because of a pectoral injury. The Eagles sent two third-round picks to the Vikings for Greenard in April and promptly gave him a four-year, $98 million contract. If he does play Monday, he’s “definitely not ready for a full workload,” Fangio said.</p><p>Greenard and receiver DeVonta Smith (hamstring) were among the Eagles players limited in Friday’s practice. Running back Saquon Barkley (stinger) and Carter (wrist) practiced in full, while receiver Hollywood Brown (ankle) and tight end Dallas Goedert (knee) sat out.</p><p>Carter and linebackers Nolan Smith and Jihad Campbell have one sack apiece; only four teams have fewer sacks than the Eagles’ three. Still, the Eagles have given up the fifth-fewest passing yards per game in the NFL this year, a product of playing the Commanders and Titans through two weeks.</p><p>The Eagles haven’t taken the ball away all year, though — something only the Commanders and Texans can say — and give up the 11<sup>th</sup>-most rushing yards in the NFL. Last year, the Bears ran for a whopping 281 yards in Philadelphia.</p><p>Asked if he wanted his players to remember that feeling, Fangio sited his own film work. Like Taylor, he knows what he’ll show his players this week.</p><p>“You ain’t going to be able to flush it away,” he said. “It’s going to be on our cutups, so we’ll see it.”<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Cubs’ final regular-season game vs. Red Sox moved from Fenway Park to Florida as storms descend on Boston
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON – The scheduling craziness of the regular season’s final series keeps coming for the Cubs.</p><p>After playing a weather-forced doubleheader against the Red Sox on Friday in Boston, it was announced that incoming storms forced the final game of the regular season to Sunday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Florida, where the two teams will finish off the campaign at Tropicana Field, the home of the Rays.</p><p>That game will start at 2:05 p.m. Central, the same time as every other game in the league on the final day of the regular season.</p><p>There could still be something to play for in that one, with the Cubs a game and a half back of the Padres in the NL wild-card standings after losing the first game of Friday’s doubleheader.</p><p>Their opening-round opponent and the location of that best-of-three series is still to be determined on the season’s final weekend. The top wild-card team will host the series, which could still be played at Wrigley Field. The second-place wild-card team will travel to play the first-place team, while the third-place wild-card team will travel to play the Braves in Atlanta.</p>
