entries.title: Illinois Supreme Court sides with widow of Uber rider killed in wrongful death case
entries.summary: <p>The ride-sharing giant, Uber, has been dealt a legal setback by a unanimous Illinois Supreme Court that sided with the widow of 60-year-old rider killed in a 2022 crash along the Stevenson Expressway.</p><p>The question at the center of the case was whether a family member of a deceased rider would be forced into third-party arbitration to settle a wrongful death or severe injury claim, rather than hashing the issue out in the courts.</p><p>In its registration process, Uber requires every user to agree to mandatory arbitration to settle any potential claims against the company.</p><p>The seven-person high court ruled Gloria Sheridan Geller, acting as a representative of the estate of her late husband, Mark Geller, is exempt from that requirement and can sue Uber for damages. That's despite Gloria Sheridan Geller also having agreed to the abitration clause as a registered Uber user herself.</p><p>“Because [her] agreement applies only to disputes arising from her own use of Uber’s services and because the estate’s wrongful death claims arise solely from Mark’s use and accrued only upon his death, no clear and unmistakable evidence exists to conclude that the parties agreed to … an arbitrator,” wrote Justice David K. Overstreet in the court’s opinion.</p><p>Uber did not return WBEZ’s requests for comment.</p><p>On April 19, 2022, Mark Geller was riding in an Uber when 51-year-old driver Ejaz Rathore lost control of the vehicle, striking a fixed object along Interstate 55 in Chicago. Both men were taken to hospitals and pronounced dead, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2022/4/20/23034385/interstate-55-crash-throop" target="_blank" ><u>according to Illinois State Police.</u></a></p><p>Geller’s widow, on behalf of his estate, nearly a year later filed a nine-count complaint in Cook County Circuit Court, arguing that Rathore was negligent and that Uber was “vicariously liable.”</p><p>Uber argued for the case’s dismissal, saying Geller's widow also agreed to arbitrate disputes when she checked the “I accept” box on the Uber app’s user agreement page “in the same manner Mark did.”</p><p>The company reported 153 motor vehicle fatalities nationwide between 2020 and 2021, according to Uber’s most recent <a class="Link" href="https://tb-static.uber.com/prod/udam-assets/25d012e2-97e1-5746-ae4a-e54c9d3dc3cd.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>safety study. </u></a></p><p>The safety of ride-sharing app users has sparked national attention in recent years.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/uber-california-death-emily-normandin-parker-7cee8b2071c5ecc4414391b8fb6004a0" target="_blank" ><u>Last week</u></a>, an arbitrator ordered Uber to pay $40 million to the parents of a 23-year-old passenger who was fatally struck by oncoming traffic after her driver pulled over to the shoulder of a highway in Southern California.</p><p>And since the app’s popularity skyrocketed, Uber has faced mounting lawsuits alleging sexual assault and misconduct by drivers against users. That same report found 2,717 incidents across the most serious categories of sexual assault and misconduct that year.</p><p>A coalition of victim advocacy groups, including the Illinois Coalition Against Sexual Assault, had filed an amicus brief in support of Geller’s widow. In their brief, the group argued for the end of forced arbitration, saying victims were “less likely to succeed, and received significantly lower awards, while the secrecy of arbitration perpetuated a "culture of silence.”</p><p>Per the court’s orders, the wrongful death case will now proceed in the circuit court system.</p><p><i>Mawa Iqbal covers state government and politics for WBEZ and Illinois Public Radio. </i></p>
entries.author: Mawa Iqbal

entries.title: Dueling renters protection measures slated for a City Council vote Tuesday
entries.summary: <p>Ald. Gilbert Villegas (36th) is turning up the heat on the battle over updating Chicago’s four-decade-old renters rights ordinance, scheduling a vote on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/27/renters-protection-ordinances-mayor-brandon-johnson-aldermanic-opponents-dueling-versions-chicago-city-council" >dueling proposals</a> at a special City Council meeting Tuesday despite his vows for “more dialogue” and compromise.</p><p>By filing his intent with the Clerk’s office to call for a vote on both proposed ordinances, one of them crafted by him, Villegas is starting a clock on negotiations and signaling to his opposition that he believes his ordinance has the votes to pass without further talks.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/16/brandon-johnson-renters-protection-ordinance-aldermen-dueling-proposals-chicago-city-council-housing-committe" >Mayor Brandon Johnson has proposed </a>the so-called Protecting Renters Ordinance, or PRO. His City Council opposition are pushing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/17/city-council-zoning-committee-dueling-renter-protection-plans-brandon-johnson-gilbert-villegas" >their own version </a>that they believe more fairly balances the needs of renters and landlords. That version is called the Fair and Accountable Illinois Rental Ordinance, or FAIR.</p><p>At a City Council meeting Wednesday, both sides agreed to hold off on calling for a vote on their respective proposals, claiming they were in favor of collaboration. </p><p>When asked what changed, Villegas said he was provoked by a move Wednesday from Ald. Jason Ervin (28th), Johnson’s most powerful ally. Ervin said it “makes no sense” that both proposals are active and requested for a compromise to be reached in a joint committee. The motion went nowhere. But Villegas said Ervin's motion put him on the spot. </p><p>“The housing advocates should be wondering why is the mayor's floor leader doing this? It's not me. It's causing me to react. I'm not the one who took the first action here,” Villegas said when asked what message he has for housing advocates who’ve worked for years on the proposal.</p><p>“When you're making an attempt like that, that gives us pause because it's like, are you being an honest broker[?],” Villegas said. </p><p></p><p>Over the past several weeks, some compromises have been made on both sides. The mayor removed from his proposal a key provision that requires landlords to pay relocation costs if they don’t renew leases. FAIR sponsors removed language from their proposal that expanded exemptions for landlords who own up to 12 units.</p><p>However, the remaining sticking points revolve around key logistical questions about how either rental protection ordinance would be enforced, what information the rental registry would collect, and how much money landlords would pay to register.</p><p>The Mayor’s proposal would create a Bureau of Rental Housing Services within the Department of Housing funded by fees collected through a new citywide rental registry. FAIR collects less information for the rental registry, does not include a fee for landlords, and assigns enforcement duties to the city’s Department of Buildings.</p><p>Villegas’ move came as a surprise to tenants’ advocates, in part because of his repeated promises, as early as last week, to hash out an agreement with the coalition opposed to his more landlord-friendly renters ordinance.</p><p>“Listen, everyone that knows me knows that I’m always willing to engage and willing to have discussions to try to get to a compromise. I don’t allow perfect to be the enemy,” Villegas told progressive Ald. Ruth Cruz at a hearing last week as she expressed concern that the rental registry in Villegas’ proposal didn’t go far enough.</p><p>“There are some similarities between the ordinances and there are some differences. And I think the only way to really get to the point where there could be an opportunity to get more support is to continue to have those discussions. You do have my word that we will continue to have dialogue,” he said.</p><p>On Friday, Villegas told WBEZ the scheduled vote “forces more dialogue,” but later said there are no negotiation meetings scheduled before Tuesday.</p><p></p><p>Tenant advocates on Friday said they were disappointed to hear of Villegas’ move.</p><p>Michelle Gilbert, an attorney at the Law Center for Better Housing, said, “We had met with Ald. Villegas earlier, and I felt that there was really a spirit of cooperation and trying to achieve the best result. Calling it for a vote at this point without further meeting or discussion is against that spirit of cooperation.”</p><p>Marty Cozzola, an attorney at Impact for Equity, said he is not aware of “any negotiation since both ordinances passed out of committee. It's pretty shocking to hear that they are both going to be called for a vote next week, when there were multiple alderpeople on the record saying they wanted changes to FAIR before they would vote in favor.” </p><p>Even if Villegas has the 26 votes needed to pass his measure, he’s also under pressure to compromise to avoid a mayoral veto. That takes 34 votes to override.</p><p></p>
entries.author: Esther Yoon-Ji Kang

entries.title: After troubled South Loop bar Reserv closes, former workers say they're still waiting to be paid
entries.summary: <p>A South Loop restaurant and bar that drew the ire of neighbors, employees and city officials permanently closed its doors.</p><p>Reserv at 744 S. Dearborn St. has relinquished its licenses, according to 4th Ward Ald. Lamont Robinson.</p><p>The move comes “after months of concerns raised by Printers Row and South Loop residents,” Robinson said in an email this week to constituents. "Our office worked to ensure residents were heard throughout the city's regulatory process."</p><p>Robinson said he would continue working to ensure "businesses and neighborhood quality of life can thrive together."</p><p>Reserv founder Gerald Joseph declined to comment.</p><p>The eatery had been facing mounting pressure to address noise complaints from neighbors and the city. Several former Reserv employees also alleged they were owed thousands of dollars in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2026/07/11/south-loop-restaurant-reserv-facing-eviction-former-workers-allege-wage-theft" >unpaid wages and tips</a>. The restaurant, open for less than a year, also faced an eviction case after failing to pay roughly $45,000 in rent, court records show.</p><p>Throughout the summer, residents complained about loud music, rooftop noise and crowds gathering outside the bar. The Chicago Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection held several hearings about the noise.</p><p>Joseph told the Chicago Sun-Times in July that he took steps to appease neighbors by disconnecting subwoofers, increasing security and raising the minimum age for some events.</p><p>But the restaurant drew scrutiny again on Aug. 23, when several fights happened outside Reserv. Videos on social media, recorded by bystanders, show a brawl spreading into bike lanes on Dearborn Street. Chicago police could be seen dispersing the crowd.</p><p>At the time, Robinson called for the venue's license to be revoked, arguing that neighbors had endured months of noise and public safety concerns.</p><p>“Our residents deserve to feel safe in their own neighborhood,” he said in a statement sent to residents. “I appreciate the officers who responded, and we will continue to work with BACP, CPD, and the community to ensure this matter is addressed appropriately and decisively.”</p><p>After the August incident, BACP issued a cease-and-desist order that required Reserv to stop hosting live music and events with cover charges.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Victor said city officials have asked Reserv’s workers to provide records of shifts worked, communications with management and attempts to obtain payment.</p><p>Victor and Townsend said they’ve found other bartending jobs since leaving Reserv earlier this year.</p><p>"I feel like he might file for bankruptcy in order to try to get out of paying us what we're owed," Townsend said of the founder.</p><p>Although she’s been encouraged by the support from neighbors, Victor said the attention surrounding Reserv's closure has done little to ease the financial strain she has experienced.</p><p>"It kind of feels like everybody is paying attention to the news more than what's actually going on with the people involved," she said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2026/07/11/south-loop-restaurant-reserv-facing-eviction-former-workers-allege-wage-theft" >South Loop restaurant Reserv facing eviction as former workers allege wage theft</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
